PROTOCOL: outcome-blind allocation-geometry census executed at zero GPU (288 legal allocations; x_C and a_A_iid deterministically coupled; matched-pair conditions 0/0; condition number 71.83>20) therefore the prewritten fallback is OPERATIVE: management-axis cube (task-count x instrument x hierarchy), dual allocation geometry exploratory only. Stage 0: common both-arm prefix to a frozen 40% task transition; full state saved bit-exact (network, optimizer moments CARRIED per frozen policy D1, BN buffers, all RNG streams, replay buffer contents and order); challenge clone measures tau_A/tau_C per frozen formula; response clones measure the signed 2x2 R[c,r]; frozen score V(r)=sum_c w_c R[c,r], S_CR=V(C)-V(A) with liveness abstention; prediction bundle sealed (hash) before endpoints mount. Stage 1: sealed A-only/C-only forks from the same parent state; one-shot adjudication. Five data identities with zero-overlap verification; any integrity failure is INVALID, never a negative. Gates frozen: NLL primary (>=7/8 block winner direction; Spearman >=0.74 exact permutation; beats x-only, 2D-geometry, management-only, response-only, and equal-budget short-run baselines on proper scoring and MAE SESOI; permuted-challenge upper-5%-tail) plus deployment-J ternary validation; five adjudication branches prewritten incl. explicit FAIL wording. Budget 76.8 full-cell equivalents, 25-30 GPU-h, hard cap 40. STATUS AT REGISTRATION: zero Stage-0 cells; zero SCTA GPU hours; no outcome of any block exists; all formula parameters either frozen or carry explicit FROZEN-BY synthetic-test placeholders bound before any GPU cell.

title: ALCS-26: A linguistically structured arabic-based lightweight cryptographic standard for secure and culturally adaptive communication
abstract: Historically, cryptography and language have shared a deep conceptual connection. Early classical ciphers, such as monoalphabetic substitutions and polyalphabetic systems, were inherently language-dependent, exploiting structural features of alphabetic systems. Yet modern cryptographic theory, particularly after Shannon’s seminal formalization of confusion and diffusion, shifted toward mathematically rigorous, language-agnostic constructions. This abstraction significantly improved provable security guarantees but removed potential entropy sources embedded within linguistic systems. Natural languages are not merely symbolic collections but structured systems characterized by orthographic rules, morphological transformations, contextual variations, and phonetic redundancy. The Arabic language, in particular, exhibits several structural characteristics that make it uniquely suitable for cryptographic modelling. Unlike Latin-based alphabets, Arabic letters adopt contextual forms depending on positional placement within a word (isolated, initial, medial, final). Moreover, diacritics (harakat) introduce optional phonetic variability without altering semantic identity in many contexts. The language also follows a triliteral root–pattern morphological system, generating extensive lexical families from limited root structures. These characteristics collectively produce an intrinsic polymorphic symbol space. Through experimental validation using representative Arabic corpora, ALCS-26 enhances ciphertext entropy, exhibits strong avalanche characteristics, and provides resistance to frequency-based cryptanalysis. The alignment of cryptographic design with linguistic structure in ALCS-26 establishes a culturally appropriate encryption paradigm for secure messaging, IoT implementations, and text-image steganographic integration in Arabic-speaking communities. This framework contributes to the emerging area of language-aware cryptographic engineering and supplements previous work on image-based secure communication systems.

title: COPA: Continual Preference Optimization for Adaptive Prompt Injection Defense
abstract: LLMs remain vulnerable to prompt injection attacks, where adversarial instructions embedded in user inputs or external content manipulate model behavior and bypass safeguards. Existing defenses are predominantly static, relying on fixed alignment objectives or attack-specific filtering mechanisms that require redesign as new attack strategies emerge. While recent lifelong alignment methods address shifting user preferences, they do not account for adaptive adversaries that continually evolve to exploit weaknesses in previously learned defenses. This limitation is particularly important in real-world deployments, where evolving attack distributions necessitate continual adaptation without sacrificing robustness to previously encountered threats. We present COPA, a continual preference optimization framework that treats prompt-injection defense as a lifelong learning problem. Instead of one-time alignment, COPA incrementally incorporates feedback from newly observed attacks via GRPO-based optimization and uses margin-weighted experience replay to retain defenses against prior attack classes. This enables continuous adaptation to emerging threats while mitigating catastrophic forgetting and preserving general-purpose model capabilities. Across lifelong prompt injection attack streams, COPA reduces attack success rate by up to 6.3x and 4.4x on average compared to state-of-the-art defenses. These results highlight continual preference optimization as an effective paradigm for defending LLMs against adaptive adversaries.

title: Size and Distance Scales in the Nucleon and in Dense Baryonic Matter
abstract: This memorial tribute to Mannque Rho follows a line of thoughts and ideas that he continuously inspired and shaped over many decades: from the two-scales picture of low-energy nucleon structure to dense and cold baryonic matter as it is realized in the cores of neutron stars. Early groundbreaking concepts are recalled and updated by recent advanced analyses of the `core' and `cloud' sizes of the nucleon. Implications for dense nuclear matter are then discussed and confronted with empirical information from Bayesian inference analyses of neutron star observables.

title: Enhancing Privacy in Federated Learning via Dual Obfuscation of Gradients and Training Images
abstract: Federated learning enables collaborative model training while keeping data locally at each client; however, recent studies have shown that training data can be reconstructed from shared model updates. To address this issue, this paper proposes a dual obfuscation method that enhances robustness against image restoration attacks by jointly obfuscating updated information and training images. The proposed method combines a robustness enhancement technique based on random binary weights, which randomly sets a portion of gradient elements to zero, with an image encryption technique. These techniques provide complementary protection by reducing the amount of original gradient information available to an attacker and the visual interpretability of reconstructed images, respectively. Furthermore, the image encryption technique allows independent keys to be used for each client and each image, avoiding explicit key sharing. Experimental results on an image classification task using a Vision Transformer (ViT) show that the proposed method reduces the visual information recovered by Attention Privacy Leakage (APRIL) under the evaluated settings without causing additional degradation in classification performance beyond that caused by image encryption. Although the proposed combination does not provide an absolute security guarantee, the results demonstrate the potential benefit of combining gradient modification and image encryption for privacy-enhanced federated learning.

title: Self-optimizing multichannel optical computing
abstract: Optical computing offers a promising route towards ultrafast and energy-efficient alternatives to conventional digital processors, though practical end-to-end realization remains a significant challenge. Among several architectural limitations, most current implementations are confined to single-channel processing, which underutilizes the inherent information capacity of light. Here we demonstrate a self-optimizing multichannel optical computing architecture based on multi-plane light conversion that natively processes RGB images and structured numerical data entirely within the optical domain. We introduce two complementary optimization strategies that enable autonomous adaptation without the need for differentiable forward models: Bayesian optimization to refine channel mixing at the input level, and a hardware-in-the-loop protocol based on self-organized criticality to navigate the high-dimensional phase landscapes. Across medical imaging, natural image classification, and regression tasks, multichannel optical preprocessing with random phase masks improves accuracy by 25–45 percentage points over raw pixel baselines, with RGB encoding consistently outperforming grayscale by 6–11 percentage points. Furthermore, our self-optimization strategies provided additional gains of 7–12 percentage points. These demonstrated capabilities establish self-optimizing multichannel optical computing as a successful proof-of-concept, paving the way for future efforts to address the system-level challenges of optical machine learning. Fatma Nur Kilinc introduce a multichannel optical computer that self-optimizes, using Bayesian tuning of input channels and a self-organized-criticality protocol to reshape its own hardware, with no differentiable model required. Multichannel processing alone lifts accuracy 25-45 points, and self-optimization adds 7-12 more.

title: MACHINE LEARNING FOR FAST AND RELIABLE SOURCE LOCATION ESTIMATION IN EARTHQUAKE EARLY WARNING
abstract: Earthquakes are among the most destructive natural disasters, causing significant loss of human lives, infrastructure, and economic resources. Fast and accurate estimation of earthquake source location is therefore essential for effective Earthquake Early Warning (EEW) systems. Conventional source-location methods generally depend on seismic-wave travel-time calculations followed by mathematical inversion, which can require considerable computational time and may be difficult to apply under real-time conditions. This research proposes a machine-learning-based approach for fast and reliable earthquake sourcelocation estimation. Historical seismic observations containing P-wave and S-wave arrival times, signal amplitude, latitude, longitude, depth, and magnitude are processed through data cleaning, missing-value handling, normalization, and feature extraction. Five supervised machine-learning algorithms, namely Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), K-Nearest Neighbours (kNN), Logistic Regression (LR), and Naive Bayes (NB), are trained and evaluated. The models are assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and confusion matrix analysis. The proposed framework aims to identify the most effective model for rapidly estimating earthquake source locations while maintaining reliable prediction performance under noisy and high-volume seismic observations. The approach demonstrates the potential of machine learning to reduce computational requirements and provide faster earthquake information for early-warning and emergency-management applications. Keywords: Earthquake Early Warning, Machine Learning, Source Location Estimation, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, K-Nearest Neighbours.

title: Hybrid Rule-Based and Anomaly Detection Model for Wholesale Sales Risk Classification
abstract: Large-scale wholesale transaction systems face increasing risks from suspicious purchasing patterns, abnormal customer behavior, and operational inconsistencies, while conventional rule-based methods may fail to identify previously unseen patterns. This study develops a decision-level hybrid risk classification model that combines expert-derived business rules with post-hoc anomaly decisions from Isolation Forest and DBSCAN. The modules are orchestrated in Apache Airflow and executed through a scheduled daily DAG for batch transaction monitoring. The model was evaluated retrospectively using 12,476 wholesale transactions recorded over 12 months in a single company. The business rules and ground-truth labels were elicited from the same expert pool; therefore, the separation between model development and evaluation was implemented at the data level through independent training, validation, and test subsets. The Hybrid Rule + Isolation Forest configuration achieved the highest accuracy at 87.5%, compared with 74.3% for the authors' rule-based baseline. The resulting 13.1-percentage-point gain should be interpreted as an internal ablation result rather than a comparison with a state-of-the-art external model. For operational efficiency, the automated workflow processed a batch of 1,000 transactions in 42 seconds, compared with approximately 3 hours of manual processing. These findings suggest that combining interpretable business rules with anomaly detection at the decision level can improve risk classification while retaining operational transparency. However, because the evaluation used data from only one wholesale company and shared expert sources for rules and labels, validation across independent companies and expert groups is required before broader generalization.

title: The Efficacy and Workload Impact of AI-Integrated Workflows vs. Traditional Human Double-Reading in Ductal Carcinoma in situ Screening: A Meta-Analysis
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Breast cancer is a commonly diagnosed malignancy among women globally and represents a major public health burden. Breast cancer screening mammography detects nearly 35% of ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) among asymptomatic women. Early detection helps with timely treatment and reduces the burden of this disease. Artificial intelligence (AI) is a potential tool to improve screening efficiency. It is being integrated into breast cancer screening to address workforce constraints, while maintaining diagnostic performance. Studies evaluating AI performance for DCIS detection within screening workflows remain limited. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the diagnostic efficacy, workload impact, and recall rates of AI-integrated screening workflows compared with traditional human double-reading approaches in detecting DCIS in breast cancer screening programmes. METHODS: A meta-analysis was performed. We searched for studies evaluating AI-integrated screening workflows vs. standard double reading in asymptomatic breast cancer screening populations. The primary outcome was the DCIS detection rate per 1,000 women screened (or per 1,000 screenings). Secondary outcomes included recall rate and workload reduction. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-AI. RESULTS: Five studies were included in the analysis. There was no significant difference in DCIS detection between AI-assisted workflows and standard double reading (pooled RR 1.17, 95% CI 0.79-1.75, I² = 82.3%, p = 0.433), with substantial heterogeneity. The outcomes for recall rates were not significantly different overall with AI use (pooled RR 1.19, 95% CI 0.87-1.62, I² = 98.6%, p = 0.275). There was a mean workload reduction of 42.9% (SD 1.5%) with AI integration. CONCLUSION: AI-integrated screening workflows can reduce workload and result in slight increases in recall rates (I² = 98.6%). However, the effect on DCIS detection (I² = 82.3%) is not clear due to heterogeneity across studies. There is a need to exercise caution in incorporating AI into the diagnostic process for DCIS until more data becomes available.

title: PAG ETR · framework reprodutível de analogia geológica para priorização de investigação geoquímica de elementos terras raras em Mato Grosso do Sul
abstract: PAG ETR is a logical, categorical, multiscale and reproducible framework for diagnosing evaluability and organizing rare-earth-element geochemical investigation hypotheses in territories with incomplete geoscientific data. The first pilot implementation in Mato Grosso do Sul preserves explicit unknown states, non-compensatory rules, provenance, independent 250, 500 and 1000 km² grids, frozen results, reproduction scripts, tests and a public cartographic interface. The reproducible package was extracted from ITA ARANDU MS to permit independent auditing of the pilot. PAG ETR does not identify deposits, resources or reserves and does not constitute field authorization.

title: Algorithmic Confluence Theory
abstract: This paper introduces the Algorithmic Confluence Theory (ACT), a framework designed to address the fundamental question of consistency across divergent execution paths within complex computational systems. Building upon concepts from program rewriting theory, ACT expands the scope to encompass a broader range of computing paradigms, including parallel computation, multi-agent systems, and large AI models. The core of ACT revolves around the 'Computational Confluence Criterion,' which aims to determine under what conditions multiple, initially disparate, computational paths will inevitably converge to a single, consistent outcome. The theory posits that the convergence is not guaranteed universally, but rather depends on specific structural properties and operational characteristics of the system. This work explores the key elements of ACT, including defining the relevant metrics for path divergence and convergence, and outlining the conditions necessary for achieving confluence. The paper provides a foundational understanding of the theory, laying the groundwork for further research and applications in diverse computational domains.

title: Computational History Principle
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational History Principle (CHP), a novel approach to understanding and modeling computation that moves beyond the traditional focus on the current state of a program. CHP posits that the complete definition of a program's state requires consideration of its entire historical trajectory. It argues that even if two states appear identical at a given point in time, if their histories diverge, they may possess fundamentally different future computational capabilities. This principle is formalized as History-sensitive Computation, emphasizing the crucial role of past events in determining future behavior. The core idea is that computation isn't just about what's happening *now*, but about how that 'now' came to be, and how that lineage will shape what *can* happen next. This concept has implications for areas such as program verification, debugging, and the design of adaptive systems.

title: Machine Learning for Anomaly Detection in Financial Business Transaction Monitoring
abstract: The detection of anomalies in the monitoring of financial transactions is an essential component in the process of identifying fraudulent or suspicious activities. Interquartile Range (IQR) is used for preprocessing, unsupervised feature learning is used for feature selection, and Support Vector Machine (SVM) is used for classification in this research study. The purpose of this paper is to offer an effective machine learning-based approach for detecting abnormalities in financial transactions. The IQR approach is utilized during the preprocessing step in order to identify and eliminate outliers. This helps to guarantee that the dataset is thorough and accurate in its representation of typical transactional patterns. Unsupervised feature learning approaches, such as autoencoders, are applied for the purpose of feature selection. These techniques are utilized to extract useful features without relying on labeled data. This enables the model to learn from the inherent patterns that are present in the acquired data.

title: PROMPT-TIME CROSS-LINGUAL TRANSFER FOR LOW-RESOURCE LANGUAGES
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can translate low-resource (LR) languages from a prompt alone, but whether this reflects genuine cross-lingual transfer or surface-cuedriven task recognition remains unclear. Using a 10-language subset of the LoResLM “Rosetta Stone” benchmark in a controlled regime where in-context demonstrations are high-resource (HR)!EN pairs and the LR language appears only in the final query, I evaluate four multilingual LLMs across six prompt conditions. Two findings qualify the linguistically diverse prompting recommendation: a single well-chosen close donor matches or outperforms typologically diverse mixtures, and close donors beat far donors in 82.5% of language–model cells (+5:0 chrF++). A mixed-effects regression over 12,320 observations identifies character trigram overlap—not genealogical distance—as the strongest predictor of translation quality. The results support interpreting prompt-time “transfer” as task location and surface-form activation. Practical guideline: prefer donors with high character level overlap over typologically diverse ones.

title: NCTAF-GCN: Node-Contrastive Topology-Adaptive Fairing Graph Convolutional Network for anomaly detection
abstract: Graph anomaly detection plays an important role in complex systems, like financial system s , social media and computer networks , for identifying malicious components. Many researchers choose graph convolutional networks (GCNs) as the backbone model to capture structural and attribute information. Nevertheless, GCNs suffer from three inherent challenges that lead to inferior performance. Firstly, over-smoothing presentation undermines the downstream task. It means node’s features mix with many neighbors’ features. Secondly, the difference of aggregation capability for nodes. High-degree nodes are prone to capture enough information in shallow layers while low-degree nodes are still lacking common features. Thirdly, GCN is sensitive to noise. Both structure and attribute deviation could cause misclassification. To address these challenges, we propose a Node-Contrastive Topology-Adaptive Fairing Graph Convolutional Network (NCTAF-GCN), a contrastive learning method, for anomaly detection. Specifically, two topology-adaptive graphs are constructed in a heuristic way . The adaptive graphs improve the original graph representation with augment ed information. Additionally, there is a feature-level attention mechanism for enhancing anomalous features. Experiments conducted on five real-world datasets indicate that the detection capability of NCTAF-GCN surpasses that of comparative baselines.

title: Mixed-State Symmetry-Protected Topology and Strong-to-Weak Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking in a Superconducting Qubit Array
abstract: This repository contains the code, data, and analysis supporting the manuscript “Mixed-State Symmetry-Protected Topology and Strong-to-Weak Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking in a Superconducting Qubit Array.” The work investigates how measurement and decoherence transform symmetry-protected topological order in a one-dimensional cluster state using a five-qubit superconducting array. It includes experimental studies of nonlocal string order under controlled dephasing, measurement-induced long-range entanglement, and mixed-state strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking. The results demonstrate average symmetry-protected topological order, a tunable transition between GHZ and separable states, and distinct long-range correlations that emerge depending on which degrees of freedom are treated as the environment and how information about them is handled.

title: CoToGrasp: Contact-Topology-Conditioned Dexterous Grasp Synthesis via Canonical Workspace Learning
abstract: Current dexterous grasp planners primarily optimize for physical stability, focusing on whether an object can be grasped rather than how it should be grasped to support downstream functional tasks. However, conditioning grasp synthesis on specific human grasp taxonomies typically requires prohibitively expensive, object-annotated datasets. To address these limitations, we propose CoToGrasp, a novel generative framework that synthesizes diverse, stable grasps strictly conditioned on specific contact topologies. To bypass the data collection bottleneck, CoToGrasp is trained entirely in an object-agnostic manner. We introduce a feature-based canonical workspace that projects local object features into a unified gripper-centric domain, effectively decoupling the semantic functional intent from the arbitrary object geometry. By learning the intrinsic contact manifold of the gripper within this workspace, our model achieves zero-shot generalization to unseen objects at inference. Extensive evaluations on the large-scale DexGraspNet dataset demonstrate that CoToGrasp achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming existing taxonomy-guided planners. Finally, we demonstrate the physical viability and kinematic feasibility of our synthesized contact topologies on a physical robot platform. Code is available on our project website https://cea-list.github.io/cotograspweb/ .

title: Computational Symmetry Breaking (计算对称破缺理论)
abstract: This paper proposes a novel theoretical framework, termed Computational Symmetry Breaking (CSB), to explain the emergence of complex cognitive abilities like reasoning, memory, and planning in artificial intelligence systems. The core premise of CSB is that initially, AI systems operate under a highly symmetrical, rule-based computational environment – a state of perfect symmetry. During the training process, this symmetrical state is gradually disrupted, leading to the emergence of asymmetry and, consequently, the capacity for higher-level cognitive functions. Mathematically, this disruption is modeled as a controlled deviation from an initial state (s₀) towards a more complex, asymmetrical state (sₒ) defined by the following equation: sₒ = f(s₀, E, T) where: * s₀ represents the initial symmetrical state. * E represents the training data and the learning algorithm. * T represents the training time. * f is a non-linear function that dictates the degree of symmetry breaking. This function can be further decomposed into several components, including: * Noise Injection (N): N = η * R(t) where η is the noise injection rate and R(t) is a random process. This introduces stochasticity into the system. * Adaptive Rule Modification (A): A = α * Δ(t) where α is the modification rate and Δ(t) represents changes to the underlying rules based on experience. * Structural Complexity Growth (S): S = β * C(t) where β is the complexity growth rate and C(t) describes the evolution of the system's internal structure. The key to the CSB framework is understanding how the controlled introduction of these elements – noise, adaptive rule modification, and structural complexity growth – drives the transition from symmetrical computation to asymmetrical computation and, ultimately, to cognitive abilities. We explore the mathematical relationships between these components and their impact on the system's evolving state. The framework posits that the 'breaking' of symmetry isn't a random event, but a carefully orchestrated process guided by the training data and the learning algorithm. Further, we examine the potential for quantifying the degree of symmetry breaking and its correlation with the performance of the AI system in tasks requiring reasoning, memory, and planning. The ultimate goal is to provide a mechanistic explanation for the observed emergence of intelligence in AI systems, moving beyond purely emergent or stochastic models.

title: Algorithm Folding Theory
abstract: This paper introduces the Algorithm Folding Theory (AFT), a novel approach to algorithm design and prediction inspired by protein folding. AFT posits that algorithms, like proteins, possess an inherent, underlying structure that dictates their behavior. Instead of focusing on explicit code implementation, AFT aims to identify and 'fold' this fundamental structure, leading to predictive algorithm design. The core concept involves defining a set of algorithmic primitives – the 'folding units' – and their relationships, mimicking the hierarchical nature of protein domains. This theoretical framework suggests that a system of rules governing the interaction of these units can, in principle, determine the overall behavior of a complex algorithm. The presented theory outlines a methodology for identifying these folding units and establishing the 'folding' rules, ultimately leading to Algorithm Folding Prediction. The limitations of current algorithmic design methodologies are highlighted, and the potential of AFT as a paradigm shift in algorithm development is discussed.

title: Universal Computational Compression Principle
abstract: This paper introduces the Universal Computational Compression Principle (UCCP), a foundational concept proposing that any genuinely effective algorithm fundamentally represents a limit compression process. The principle aims to unify complexity, learning, and reasoning by establishing a core compression framework. This document outlines the core tenets of the UCCP, detailing its implications for algorithm design and theoretical understanding of computation. The central argument revolves around the inherent efficiency of compression – reducing data while retaining essential information – as a driving force behind intelligent systems. We explore the mathematical underpinnings of this perspective, focusing on the concept of information entropy and its role in defining and measuring compression effectiveness. The goal is to provide a robust theoretical basis for understanding computational processes and potentially inspire novel algorithmic approaches. ---

title: Computational Deferred Causality
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Computational Deferred Causality (CDC), a framework for modeling and analyzing systems where the ultimate effect on a system is not immediately determined by initial conditions but emerges over time. Traditional causal models often assume instantaneous influence, which is insufficient for describing complex dynamic systems. CDC proposes a novel approach using Deferred Causal Graphs (DCGs) to represent these systems. DCGs explicitly account for delays in causal relationships, allowing for a more accurate depiction of how initial events propagate and ultimately influence a system's state. The core idea is that a system's behavior isn't solely defined by its immediate causes, but by the cumulative effect of causal influences that unfold over a temporal horizon. This framework provides a tool for understanding and predicting behavior in systems ranging from biological networks to economic models, where significant delays and feedback loops are prevalent. The paper outlines the theoretical foundations of CDC, details the construction and properties of DCGs, and discusses potential applications.

title: From Rule Engines to Ontologies: An OWL 2 DL Approach for Domain-Specific Evaluation Information Systems
abstract: Domain-specific information systems often maintain their data model, rule base, and application infrastructure as separate artifacts, complicating maintenance and pre-deployment verification. This study investigates whether these artifacts can be unified in a verifiable ontology-to-code pipeline without changing the expected classifications. The proposed Model-Driven Architecture uses the Business Application Builder framework and a Web Ontology Language 2 Description Logic ontology to represent domain structure, classification rules, and generation metadata. HermiT verifies consistency, satisfiability, and subsumption under open-world semantics before code generation. The generator produces persistence, business-logic, data-transfer, and presentation layers, while the generated Java application evaluates stored records under closed-world semantics and resolves overlapping categories using ontology-declared priorities. In a Serbian research-evaluation case study, the generated system reproduced the M30 and M33 classifications of an established Jess implementation. An internal secondary experiment generated and executed a prenatal-diagnosis application; all six runtime classifications matched the HermiT entailments and expected outcomes. The public artifact independently reproduces the ontology-level experiments but excludes the proprietary generator and generated source code. The results support the feasibility of ontology-driven generation for static-classification systems, whereas arithmetic risk computation and temporal event processing remain better suited to complementary procedural technologies. No performance superiority is claimed.

title: Retrieval Beats Cheap Structured Memory: A Cost–Retention Study of LLM Agent Memory on Real Long-Conversation Benchmarks
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents that resend an expanding conversation history incur token costs that grow quadratically over a multi-turn task. Many memory designs promise to bound this cost, but their retention/cost trade-offs are frequently measured only on short or synthetic data. This paper is a controlled cost–retention study of seven memory strategies—full context, truncation, running summary, append-only notes, cheap-extractor fact slots, sparse BM25 retrieval, and a slots+retrieval hybrid—evaluated on real, human-annotated long-conversation benchmarks (LoCoMo and LongMemEval) with an LLM-as-judge protocol and question-level paired statistics. Three findings emerge. First, BM25 retrieval is the strongest cheap memory: on LoCoMo (n=160 questions over conversations of 369–680 turns) it cuts real input tokens by 98% and cost to 4.8% of full context while holding retention level with it (39.4% vs. 30.6% point estimates; paired sign test p=0.09, a nonsignificant trend whose confirmation a power analysis places at ≈360–430 questions), and it is significantly better than truncation (p<0.001). Second, we report a negative result with a diagnosis: latest-value fact slots written by a cheap 8B extractor—a structured memory we hypothesized would excel at fact updates—are the weakest memory method on both benchmarks, including on LongMemEval’s knowledgeupdate category (n=72; 37.5% vs. 73.6% for retrieval). An extractor-size ablation isolates the cause: swapping the 8B extractor for a 70B model raises slot retention by +29.2 points (paired sign test, 23 wins vs. 2 losses, p<10−4 ), showing the extractor, not the slot representation, is the bottleneck—but the stronger extractor costs 1.8× full context on these histories, so the cheap-cascade premise itself is what fails. Third, an error analysis over all 281 LoCoMo multi-hop questions shows sparse retrieval recovers only ∼13% of gold evidence turns, localizing exactly where retrieval-based memory still fails. A further LongMemEval evaluation over temporal, multi-session, and abstention questions (n=254) sharpens the boundary of the claim: on these short-history, dispersed-evidence categories full context leads, BM25 trails it significantly (−10.2 points, p=0.004), and only the slots+retrieval hybrid stays statistically indistinguishable from it—so retrieval-based memory is the right trade at long horizons and point lookups, not universally. We release the full harness, benchmark adapters, judge, and per-question results.

title: Wrong-Physics Backdoors in Neural PDE Operators
abstract: Neural PDE operators are increasingly trained on reusable solver archives, yet validation often relies on clean prediction error and parameter-agnostic plausibility checks. We introduce cross-parameter relinking, a data-poisoning primitive that makes a triggered input select a valid solution from the same PDE family under an incorrect physical parameter. We term this a wrong-physics backdoor: the output remains physically plausible but is wrong for the intended parameter. The attack exploits tensor-to-parameter provenance failures in multi-parameter archives by stamping the surrogate input and relinking its supervision to a cached alternate-parameter solution for the same latent sample. Across 476 attack campaigns, we evaluate Burgers, advection-diffusion, two-dimensional Navier-Stokes, and an elliptic Poisson case. Fourier Neural Operators and DeepONet provide the primary evidence, with Transformer, GRU, and LSTM models as support. FNO reaches a backdoor success rate of 1.0000 on both advection-diffusion and two-dimensional Navier-Stokes while retaining low clean relative L2 error. Clean-label, label-only, and shuffled controls show that high attack success alone is insufficient: successful attacks must move predictions toward the intended alternate-physics target while preserving bounded clean error. These results expose a structural validation gap: smoothness or generic solver-like behavior is insufficient unless the provenance of the intended physical parameter is also verified.

title: GOAG: Generative and Object-Agnostic Grasp Planner for Dexterous Robotic Manipulation
abstract: Multifingered grasping is a crucial robotic skill, but current deep-learning grasp planners often struggle to generalize to new objects because they are trained on limited, object-specific datasets. We introduce a fundamentally different approach, grounded in the observation that the gripper and the object share identical surface geometry at their mutual contact points. We propose GOAG: Generative and Object-Agnostic Grasp Planner for Dexterous Robotic Manipulation, a novel deep generative model that learns a compact latent representation of a specific gripper's contact surface distribution, enabling the efficient sampling of valid grasp configurations without relying on object-specific training data. We show that by introducing object features only at inference time, our model can effectively retrieve admissible contact areas that are compatible with the gripper's capabilities. We validate our approach through extensive experiments on established grasp protocols in both simulated and real-world scenarios, demonstrating its effectiveness with different grippers from the literature. Our method delivers state-of-the-art results on the objects from the MultiDex dataset, achieving an average success rate of 86.93%. It offers significantly faster processing when generating numerous grasps, while matching the performance of leading approaches specifically trained on this dataset. Unlike these methods, our approach does not rely on object-specific training data, highlighting the advantages of object-agnostic learning. It effectively addresses the generalization challenges faced by traditional data-driven grasp planners. Code and videos are available on our project website https://cea-list.github.io/goagweb/ .

title: Non-Markovianity induced by Pauli twirling
abstract: Abstract Noise forms a central obstacle to effective quantum information processing. Recent experimental advances enable noise tailoring through Pauli twirling, transforming arbitrary noise channels into Pauli channels. This is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computation, noise characterization, and error mitigation. Pauli-Lindblad channels aptly parameterize quasi-local Pauli channels, where negative Pauli-Lindblad parameters have been excluded on the basis of Markovianity of the noise processes. We study how Pauli twirling affects Markovianity using two established notions, which we term channel semigroup Markovianity for channels and Markovianity by divisibility for channel families. We prove that (1) any Pauli channel with nonzero Pauli eigenvalues admits a Pauli-Lindblad parameterization if complex Pauli-Lindblad parameters are allowed, and (2) a Pauli channel with strictly positive and nondegenerate eigenvalues fails to be channel semigroup Markovian if and only if at least one of its Pauli-Lindblad parameters is negative. Using this, we show that Pauli twirling can break channel semigroup Markovianity, even when the underlying noise process is Markovian by divisibility, an important example being the standard implementation of the $$\sqrt{X}$$ X gate. Thus, allowing negative or even nonreal Pauli-Lindblad parameters is necessary for correct noise descriptions in experimentally relevant scenarios, with direct implications for quantum error mitigation protocols that rely on accurate noise characterization.

title: LARGE LANGUAGE MODEL DENGAN RETRIEVAL AUGMENTED GENERATION PADA SISTEM TANYA JAWAB DOKUMEN PERUNDANG-UNDANGAN KETENAGAKERJAAN INDONESIA
abstract: Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mengembangkan sistem tanya jawab dokumen undang-undang ketenagakerjaan agar meningkatkan kualitas jawaban dari pertanyaan yang berkaitan dengan ketenagakerjaan. Sistem dikembangkan menggunakan LLaMA 3.1-8B-Instruct yang di-fine-tuning dengan metode Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) dan diintegrasikan dengan Retrieval Augmented Generation untuk meningkatkan relevansi jawaban berdasarkan dokumen sumber. Evaluasi dilakukan dengan membandingkan 3 model yakni model baseline, baseline dengan RAG, serta model fine-tuning dengan RAG menggunakan metrik ROUGE dan BERTScore. Hasil pengujian menunjukkan model baseline dengan RAG memperoleh performa terbaik. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan penerapan RAG mampu meningkatkan kualitas jawaban dibandingkan model baseline, namun proses fine-tuning yang dilakukan belum mampu melampaui performa model baseline dengan RAG. This study aims to develop a question-answering system for Indonesian labor law documents to improve the quality of responses to labor-related questions. The proposed system is built using LLaMA 3.1-8B-Instruct, which is fine-tuned using the Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) method and integrated with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to enhance response relevance by leveraging information retrieved from source documents. The system is evaluated by comparing three models: the baseline model, the baseline model with RAG, and the fine-tuned model with RAG. Performance is assessed using the ROUGE and BERTScore evaluation metrics. The experimental results show that the baseline model with RAG achieves the best overall performance. The findings indicate that integrating RAG significantly improves answer quality compared to the baseline model. However, the fine-tuning process employed in this study does not outperform the baseline model with RAG.

title: Algorithmic Granularity Invariance
abstract: This paper explores the concept of Algorithmic Granularity Invariance (AGI), a theoretical framework examining the inherent properties of algorithms that remain consistent irrespective of the level of detail employed in their representation. The core idea posits that a given algorithm, regardless of whether it is described through a series of micro-steps, a single high-level operation, or a mathematical function, possesses a fundamental invariance with respect to its granularity. This work formalizes this concept using the indicator function `I_G(C)`, which denotes the degree of granularity invariance for a computational process `C`. The paper presents a foundational definition: `I_G(C_{fine})=I_G(C_{coarse})`, arguing that if two representations of the same algorithm – one with fine-grained detail and another with coarse-grained detail – yield identical computational outcomes, then the algorithm exhibits AGI. The investigation focuses on identifying the key characteristics that contribute to AGI, laying the groundwork for future research into algorithm design, optimization, and verification methodologies. The paper aims to establish a rigorous theoretical basis for understanding and leveraging granularity invariance in various computational domains.

title: Algorithmic Precedence Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Algorithmic Precedence Theory (APT), a novel framework for analyzing and designing complex systems. Traditional approaches to algorithm selection often focus on comparing the *performance* of algorithms – speed, memory usage, accuracy – but fail to address a fundamentally important question: *what order must calculations occur in for a system to function correctly?* APT posits that the order of computational steps (precedence) is a critical determinant of system behavior, forming a new mathematical structure worthy of investigation. The theory is built around the notation `A ⟷ B`, where `A` represents a computational step and `B` represents another computational step, signifying that `A` must precede `B`. This paper outlines the core principles of APT, explores its potential applications across diverse domains, and lays the groundwork for future research into this previously underappreciated aspect of system design. The theory offers a shift in perspective, moving beyond simple algorithm comparison to a focus on the inherent dependencies and logical ordering of computation. ---

title: Task-Specific QLoRA Adaptation in RAG-Based Information Extraction from Research Articles
abstract: Large Language Models have shown considerable potential for academic document understanding, but their use in information extraction remains limited by hallucination and incomplete evidence grounding. This study presents an end-to-end Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework using a domain-adapted Llama 3.1 8B Instruct model. Generation reliability is evaluated through faithfulness, answer relevancy, context precision, and context recall, while retrieval relevance is measured using a rank-based percentile score that supports comparison across cosine, dot-product, and Euclidean similarity functions. Context recall is computed through a reference-free and answer-dependent procedure and is therefore interpreted as the extent to which the information expressed in an answer is accounted for by the supplied context. Experiments were conducted on 100 research articles using three tasks: research objective extraction, methodological information extraction, and experimental result interpretation. A separate QLoRA adapter was trained for each task, and the base and adapted models were evaluated under identical retrieval and generation conditions across three embedding models and three similarity functions. Under the highest-scoring configuration for each task, the composite score increased from 0.809 to 0.821, from 0.807 to 0.818, and from 0.795 to 0.814, respectively. The adapted model achieved a composite score in 26 of 27 task–retrieval configurations, although only the experimental-result task remained statistically significant after false discovery rate correction. Error analysis showed fewer fabricated statements and less task drift than the base model.

title: Differentially Private Continual Release with Relative Error
abstract: This work investigates several fundamental tasks, including $\mathsf{MaxSum}$, $\mathsf{MinSum}$, $\mathsf{MaxSelect}$, and $\mathsf{MinSelect}$, in the continual release model under differential privacy. Previous research has demonstrated that any algorithm for these tasks must admit a large purely additive error. We show that the error can be substantially reduced if a relative error term is allowed, provided that the input stream is generated non-adaptively. However, when input data records can be selected adaptively, we prove that a large error is inevitable for the task of selecting an attribute with a small cumulative sum, whereas small error bounds remain achievable for other tasks. This reveals a significant separation between non-adaptive and adaptive streams. We also complement our algorithms with nearly matching lower bounds.

title: Tracking the Trend in How Speech Synthesizers Deceive People
abstract: Advances in speech synthesis have made deepfake audio highly realistic. Earlier studies reported 70-80% human detection accuracy, but relied primarily on older synthesizers. We compare human detection for three selected voice synthesis tools released in 2019, 2022, and 2024 with 82 IT professionals, and benchmark humans against six pretrained detectors on the same material. For fully synthetic speech (full spoofs), the F1 score drops from about 90% for RTVC and YourTTS to 48% for ElevenLabs, although listeners were explicitly warned that deepfakes were present. For partial spoofing, where only one sentence of an utterance is altered, strict accuracy falls to 9%, and listeners classify the synthetic sentence as bona fide 77% of the time. Humans and detectors fail in complementary ways, and neither reliably localizes short manipulations. Additionally, listeners increasingly mislabel bona fide speech as fake, eroding trust in unmanipulated audio. These findings show that human perception alone is unreliable for the selected modern and partial-spoof conditions and motivate procedural verification, provenance, watermarking, and segment-level detection.

title: Adaptive encodings for small and fast compressed suffix arrays
abstract: Compressed suffix arrays index large repetitive collections and are widely used in bioinformatics, version control, and natural language processing. The \(r\) -index and its variants combine the run-length Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT) with a sample of the suffix array to achieve space proportional to the number of equal-symbol runs. While effective for near-identical strings, their size grows quickly when edited copies are added to the collection as the number of BWT runs is sensitive to variation. Existing approaches either apply extra compression at the cost of slower queries or prioritize speed at the expense of space, limiting practical tradeoffs at large scale. We introduce variable-length blocking (VLB), an adaptive encoding for BWT-based compressed suffix arrays. Our technique adapts the amount of indexing information to the local run structure: compressible regions retain less auxiliary data, while incompressible areas store more. Specifically, we recursively partition the BWT until each block contains at most \(w\) runs (a parameter), and organize the blocks into a tree. Accessing a position requires descending a root-to-leaf path followed by a short run scan. Compressible regions are placed near the root, while incompressible regions lie deeper and are augmented with additional indexing data to speed up access. This strategy balances space and query speed by reallocating bits saved in compressible areas to accelerate access to incompressible ones. The VLB-tree also improves memory locality by co-locating related BWT and suffix array information. Backward search relies on rank and successor queries over the BWT. We introduce a sampling technique that relaxes global correctness by guaranteeing that these queries are correct only along valid backward-search states. This restriction reduces space usage without affecting the speed or correctness of pattern matching. We further extend the concepts of the VLB-tree to encode suffix array samples and then to the subsampled \(r\) -index ( \(sr\) -index), thus producing a small fully functional compressed suffix array. Experiments show that VLB-tree variants outperform the \(r\) -index and \(sr\) -index in query time, while retaining space close to that of the \(sr\) -index. The move data structure, a recent encoding, is faster than the VLB-tree but uses considerably more space, yielding a clear space-time tradeoff.

title: CHATBOT RAG-LLM BERGUARDRAIL GANDA DENGAN CHUNKING HIERARKIS UNTUK DOKUMEN HUKUM-INSTITUSIONAL JDIH UPI
abstract: Penelitian ini merancang dan mengevaluasi chatbot berbasis Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) dengan Large Language Model (LLM) untuk mendukung pencarian pada 922 dokumen Jaringan Dokumentasi dan Informasi Hukum (JDIH) Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia (UPI). Sistem menggabungkan strategi chunking yang dapat dikonfigurasi (hierarchical small-to-big sebagai default, fixed-size sebagai alternatif), Input Validation Module (IVM) untuk keamanan dan relevansi domain, serta Response Assessment Module (RAM) berbasis Natural Language Inference untuk menilai dukungan bukti per proposisi. Pada locked test keamanan, IVM Qwen3-14B mencapai akurasi 98,1%, attack-pass 3,75%, dan false-block 0%. Prompt Guard hasil fine-tuning mencapai akurasi 99,17% dan 94,93% pada dua slice held-out yang ditulis manusia, sementara versi base meloloskan lebih dari separuh serangan pada data yang sama. Ablasi chunking tidak menunjukkan keunggulan hierarchical yang konsisten karena hasilnya bergantung pada konfigurasi pipeline. Konfigurasi RAM terbaik mencapai Macro-F1 0,563 untuk klasifikasi hubungan kalimat-bukti. Angka tersebut menunjukkan perbaikan terukur pada kondisi uji, tetapi hasilnya tidak menjamin perilaku yang sama di luar distribusi evaluasi. This research designs and evaluates a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) chatbot using Large Language Models to support search across 922 Legal Documentation and Information Network (JDIH) documents at Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia (UPI). The system combines a configurable chunking strategy (hierarchical small-to-big by default, fixed-size as a selectable alternative), an Input Validation Module (IVM) for safety and domain relevance, and a Natural Language Inference based Response Assessment Module (RAM) that assesses proposition-level evidence support. On the locked safety test, Qwen3-14B IVM achieved 98.1% accuracy, a 3.75% attack-pass rate, and a 0% false-block rate. A fine-tuned Prompt Guard reached 99.17% and 94.93% accuracy on two held-out human-written slices, where the base model passed more than half of the attacks on the same data. The chunking ablation showed no consistent hierarchical advantage, as the outcome depends on pipeline configuration. The best RAM configuration reached a Macro-F1 of 0.563 for sentence-evidence relation classification. These measurements support improvements under the test conditions, but the results do not guarantee equivalent behavior outside the evaluation distribution.

title: Replication package for "Corruption of Language Model Alerts in the Medical Internet of Things: A Functional Taxonomy and the Limits of Text-Based Risk Metrics"
abstract: Code, derived data and complete results supporting the empirical section of the manuscript "Corruption of Language Model Alerts in the Medical Internet of Things: A Functional Taxonomy and the Limits of Text-Based Risk Metrics". The package contains 774 alerts generated by a 7-billion-parameter instruction model from three corpora of clinical text, under three levels of controlled context truncation, together with the metric values, statistical analyses and latency measurements reported in the paper. Source corpora are not redistributed: only record identifiers, derived context conditions and generated alerts are included. See README for the full file inventory, the execution environment, and instructions for re-running the campaign. Version 2 adds an English translation of the campaign synthesis, provided alongside the original French document.

title: Algorithmic Trace Compression
abstract: Algorithmic Trace Compression (ATC) addresses the challenge of efficiently representing large execution traces generated by algorithms. Given a trace $\tau = (t_1, t_2, ..., t_n)$, where $t_i$ represents a timestamp or event, the goal of ATC is to identify a compressed trace $\tau^*$ such that $X(\tau^*) = X(\tau)$, where $X(\cdot)$ is a function that defines the similarity or equivalence between two traces. This work explores the theoretical foundations of ATC, focusing on minimizing the execution footprint while preserving the essential computational properties of the original trace. The core concept involves compressing not data, but the minimal execution traces needed to represent a given computation fact. This compression is critical in scenarios where trace storage and transmission are bottlenecks, particularly in parallel and distributed computing environments. The theoretical framework presented here lays the groundwork for developing practical ATC algorithms and techniques.

title: Information Conservation of Meaning
abstract: This paper investigates the fundamental challenge of preserving meaning during information transfer, particularly in scenarios involving data alteration and format changes. The core argument is that while the superficial aspects of information – its representation and form – can evolve, the underlying semantic structures, or meaning, must remain intact for successful communication and integration. We introduce the "Meaning Conservation Law," a theoretical framework designed to guide research in areas such as translation, model migration, knowledge distillation, and AI alignment. The law posits that maintaining meaning necessitates identifying and mitigating shifts in semantic representation, focusing on the preservation of relationships and dependencies within the information's conceptual structure. We explore potential metrics for quantifying meaning conservation and discuss the implications of violations for downstream tasks. The paper concludes with a call for further research into developing robust methods for ensuring meaning is consistently preserved across diverse information transfer processes.

title: Quantum Circuit Simulation of Two-Flavor Neutrino Oscillation: Noise Robustness, Error Mitigation, and Validation on Real Quantum Hardware
abstract: This project investigates whether a minimal single-qubit quantum circuit can accurately reproduce two-flavor neutrino oscillation probabilities, and quantifies the circuit's noise robustness in both simulation and on real IBM Quantum hardware. Using atmospheric-channel parameters from NuFit 6.0, an exact statevector circuit matches the analytical oscillation formula to floating-point precision (MAE ≈ 6.8×10⁻¹⁷), and a combined noise model (averaged over 5 random seeds) places the circuit's failure threshold at severity 1.143 ± 0.017; converting this to a real-hardware safety margin is sensitive to calibration choice, with plausible estimates ranging from roughly 1× to roughly 38× current hardware noise. A repeated 4-trial paired statistical test on real IBM Quantum hardware (ibm_marrakesh) found no significant effect of standard error-mitigation techniques (dynamical decoupling, gate twirling; p = 0.523) — reversing an initial single-trial result and illustrating why repeated trials are needed on noisy NISQ hardware. This archive contains all three Jupyter notebooks (classical baseline, ideal qubit simulation, noise/hardware validation), raw hardware measurement data, the full research paper, and a research log documenting every finding, correction, and methodological lesson from the project.

title: Leveraging Survey-Informed LLM Personas to Identify Cultural References : Enhancing Inclusivity in News Reporting
abstract: With increasingly mobile and diverse audiences, newsrooms worldwide face the growing challenge of addressing the needs of, and fostering meaningful connections with, a wide range of audience segments. We explore the possibility of using LLM personas to support inclusivity in news writing by identifying cultural references in news reports which pose challenges for non-native news readers. We design and implement a pipeline for building and evaluating persona of specific groups (international students, knowledge workers and non-knowledge workers) within non-native news readers in two modes: (1) minimal demographics (occupation, age) and (2) demographics plus survey-derived information. The results demonstrate that persona-driven prompting can support inclusivity in journalism, albeit with certain limitations. Qualitative evaluation showed reasonable alignment between LLM outputs prompted with the same persona, and improvement in LLM performance with additional prompt inputs based on survey data. The present results show, for the first time, empirical analysis of the application of LLM personas in identifying cultural references. Our approach can be useful for journalists to receive regular and on-the-go feedback on culturally complex references, which might require simplification or additional explanation, thus making news reports better accessible for diverse audience.

title: A logical and reproducible geological-analogy model for diagnosing evaluability and prioritizing geochemical investigation of rare earth elements in data-incomplete territories Application to Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil
abstract: Territories with uneven geoscientific coverage pose a central problem for mineral investigation because missing information may be mistaken for negative evidence, while the accumulation of proxies may produce high classifications even when necessary geological requirements remain unknown. This study presents PAG ETR as a logical, categorical, multiscale, and reproducible framework for diagnosing evaluability and organizing geochemical investigation hypotheses for rare earth elements, accompanied by a deliberately partial spatial proof of concept in Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil. The method organizes eleven mineralizing models, M1 to M11, and distinguishes TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN, CONFLICT, and NA, retaining SEM_DADO and INDETERMINADO as states of unknown information rather than absence. Progression among N0, non-evaluable, N1, open model, N2, justified targeted geochemical investigation, N3, compatible local evidence, and N4, local contradiction, is governed by non-compensatory rules and by the functions REQ, SUP, and CONF. The 250, 500, and 1,000 km² grids are evaluated independently. The conceptual library contains eleven models, but the spatial proof of concept materialized only M2 and M4 and classified 49 of 1,554 cells as N1 at 250 km², 37 of 793 at 500 km², and 24 of 412 at 1,000 km². No cell reached N2 or N3 in the spatial snapshot. This result is not interpreted as low potential but as a limit on the evaluability of the materialized evidence. A sensitivity scenario for M4 showed that 38, 28, and 17 N1 cells remain when point phosphorus records are excluded and only polygonal phosphorite units are considered. Computational reproduction recovered the same sets of hex_id and 15 executable tests returned PASS. These tests demonstrate logical consistency and determinism of the snapshot, not predictive validity. PAG ETR does not predict the location of deposits, resources, or reserves. In this version, the product should be interpreted as a diagnosis of evaluability and knowledge gaps rather than as a regional prospectivity map. Its contribution is to make explicit when a hypothesis can be opened, tested, supported, or contradicted, and when the available information remains insufficient. Field validation, independent predictive validation, and quantitative comparison with alternative methods remain future steps.

title: Universal weakly fault-tolerant quantum computation via code switching in the [[8,3,2]] code
abstract: Code switching offers a route to universal, fault-tolerant quantum computation by circumventing the limitation implied by the Eastin-Knill theorem against a universal transversal gate set within a single quantum code. Here, we present a fault-tolerant code-switching protocol between two versions of the [ [ 8 , 3 , 2 ] ] code. One version supports weakly fault-tolerant single-qubit Clifford gates, while the other supports a logical CCZ ¯ gate via transversal T / T † together with logical CZ ¯ , CNOT ¯ , and SWAP ¯ gates. Because both codes have distance 2, the protocol operates in a postselected, error-detecting regime: Single faults lead to detectable outcomes, and accepted runs exhibit quadratic suppression of logical error rates. This yields a universal scheme for postselected fault-tolerant computation. We validate the protocol numerically through simulations of state preparation, interblock logical teleportation, code switching, and a three-logical-qubit implementation of Grover's search.

title: RecPFN: Prior-Fitted Networks for In-Context-Based Recommendations
abstract: We introduce RecPFN, a prior-fitted network that brings in-context learning to sequential recommendation. RecPFN is pretrained entirely on synthetic clickstream environments sampled from a broad structural causal prior, enabling it to amortize Bayesian-style inference from a small support set. At inference, a lightweight decoder-only transformer conditions on a handful of domain sequences and produces next-item predictions for queries in a single forward pass, without any weight updates. Across eight public benchmarks, RecPFN achives state-of-the-art zero-shot performance while remaining strongly competitive with supervised methods in low-compute and low-data regimes. It is deployment-efficient and robust to domain shift, outperforming strong zero-shot baselines that rely on large real-interaction corpora. RecPFN provides a practical path toward generalizable, data-efficient recommenders and opens avenues for richer priors, longer-context ICL, and multimodal extensions. Code for training and evaluation is publicly available at https://github.com/SAP-samples/tabular-ai-recpfn/.

title: IMPLEMENTASI SISTEM REWARD DAN PUNISHMENT PENILAIAN PERILAKU SISWA ADAPTIF MENGGUNAKAN METODE FUZZY LOGIC
abstract: Penilaian perilaku siswa di sekolah menengah pada umumnya masih mengandalkan sistem poin konvensional yang kaku dan hanya menangkap dimensi kedisiplinan, tanpa mempertimbangkan dimensi perilaku sosial yang dapat diamati oleh teman sebaya. Penelitian ini bertujuan merancang dan mengimplementasikan model Fuzzy Mamdani yang mengintegrasikan data observasi sekolah yang objektif dengan data penilaian sejawat yang subjektif ke dalam satu skor akhir perilaku yang adaptif, menggunakan model ADDIE (Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, Evaluation). Model melibatkan tiga variabel input, yaitu persentase kehadiran (X1), poin perilaku kumulatif (X2), dan skor penilaian sejawat (X3), distandarkan ke semesta [0, 100] dan diproses melalui 27 aturan IF-THEN tanpa dead zone serta defuzzifikasi centroid diskrit, menghasilkan empat kategori keluaran: Perlu Pembinaan, Cukup, Baik, dan Sangat Baik. Sistem diposisikan sebagai Sistem Pendukung Keputusan (Decision Support System) yang memberikan rekomendasi skor bagi wali kelas, bukan eksekusi otomatis, dan dilengkapi elemen gamifikasi berupa poin, kategori, grafik tren, serta tujuh lencana pencapaian untuk mendorong motivasi siswa. Model diimplementasikan sebagai sistem web SiPandu berbasis Next.js dan Supabase, diuji coba pada Kelas X-9 SMAN 13 Bandung (39 siswa). Pengujian fungsional black-box menunjukkan keberhasilan 100% (20/20 skenario), sedangkan pengujian usabilitas System Usability Scale dari 17 responden menghasilkan skor rata-rata 65,88 (kategori OK/Marginal). Simulasi manual membuktikan sifat adaptif sistem melalui mekanisme kompensasi antarvariabel. Instrumen penilaian sejawat (X3) divalidasi melalui validitas isi berdasarkan pertimbangan guru Bimbingan Konseling sebagai pakar domain, dengan kelima aspek penilaian dirumuskan mengacu pada dimensi profil lulusan dalam Permendikdasmen No. 10 Tahun 2025. Penelitian ini menyimpulkan bahwa model fuzzy mamdani berhasil diimplementasikan sebagai purwarupa sistem pendukung keputusan yang adaptif untuk penilaian perilaku siswa. Student behavior assessment in secondary schools generally relies on a rigid conventional point system limited to the discipline dimension, without accounting for peer-observable social behavior. This study designs and implements a fuzzy mamdani model integrating objective school data with subjective peer assessment into a single adaptive behavior score, using the ADDIE model. The model involves three input variables, namely attendance percentage (X1), cumulative behavior points (X2), and peer assessment score (X3), standardized to a universe of [0, 100] and processed through 27 IF-THEN rules without dead zones and discrete centroid defuzzification, yielding four categories: Needs Guidance, Fair, Good, and Excellent. The system functions as a Decision Support System providing score recommendations for homeroom teachers rather than automated execution, and incorporates gamification elements, points, categories, trend graphs, and seven achievement badges, to motivate students. The model was implemented as a web-based system called SiPandu using Next.js and Supabase, piloted in Class X-9 of SMAN 13 Bandung with 39 students. Functional black-box testing showed a 100% success rate across 20 scenarios, while usability testing via the System Usability Scale from 17 respondents yielded a mean score of 65.88, categorized as OK/Marginal. Manual simulation demonstrated the system's adaptive nature through compensation mechanisms among input variables. The peer assessment instrument (X3) was validated for content validity through expert judgment from the school counselor, with its five dimensions formulated based on graduate profile dimensions in Ministerial Regulation No. 10 of 2025. This study concludes that the Fuzzy Mamdani model was successfully implemented as an adaptive decision support system prototype for student behavior assessment.

title: Computational Completion Algebra
abstract: This paper introduces and develops the framework of Computational Completion Algebra (CCA), a novel algebraic system designed to model and analyze the complexities of computational processes and their dependencies. The core of CCA rests on two fundamental operations: combination calculation (denoted as C1 ⊕ C2) and completion dependency (denoted as C1 ⇒ C2). The research focuses on establishing algebraic relationships between the completion of combined computations and the completion of individual components. Specifically, the paper investigates the relationship between Complete(C1 ⊕ C2) and Complete(C1),Complete(C2). The ultimate goal is to construct the Completion Algebra (CCA), a formalized algebraic structure that can be used to represent and manipulate computational workflows with a high degree of precision. This work lays the groundwork for future research in areas such as workflow optimization, task scheduling, and verification of complex computational systems.

title: Computational Ecology
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of "Algorithm Ecology," a novel framework for understanding the complex interactions within the rapidly evolving landscape of artificial intelligence algorithms. Rather than viewing algorithmic competition as the primary dynamic, this work posits that algorithms exist within a symbiotic ecosystem, analogous to biological food chains. We explore dependencies between various algorithms – including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Transformers, and Diffusion models – examining how their survival and success are contingent upon their relationships with other algorithms. This framework provides a new lens through which to analyze algorithmic innovation, adaptation, and ultimately, the trajectory of AI development. The core hypothesis is that algorithm evolution is best understood by treating it as an emergent property of interconnected systems, rather than solely as a result of individual optimization. Key concepts explored include algorithmic niche partitioning, co-evolutionary dynamics, and the potential for algorithmic extinction. The paper concludes with a call for further research into building a comprehensive model of Algorithm Ecology.

title: Computational Mutation Law
abstract: This paper investigates the principles governing mutation within computational systems, moving beyond traditional continuous models. The core argument posits that significant evolutionary advancements arise not from widespread, gradual changes, but from a relatively small number of structural mutations. We introduce and formalize the "Mutation Probability Equation," a key element in understanding this process. The research highlights the discrete nature of mutation events and argues for a shift in perspective regarding evolutionary algorithms. The work aims to provide a framework for analyzing and potentially optimizing evolutionary processes by focusing on the impact of targeted structural changes.

title: Sentiment Analysis and Customer Behavior Prediction in Business Using Machine Learning Frameworks
abstract: In today's world, to improve user experience and take effective decisions, understanding customer sentiment and predicting their behavior are paramount for customer businesses. This research tries to deep learning based approach for sentiment analysis and customer behavior prediction using Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT). We fine tune all them BERT models, writing on top pre trained transformers from Hugging Face. The paper proves that transformer based models outperform the conventional machine learning approaches in getting the small nuances and behavioral patterns of emotions. This work proposes a framework based on state of the art NLP techniques and deep learning architectures which can achieve very high accuracy in the sentiment classification and behavioral forecasting problems. The experimental results prove the effectiveness of real time BERT deployment for business purposes to enhance the customer engagement.

title: Beyond End-to-End Success: Diagnosing Failures in Long-Horizon Security LLM Agents
abstract: Long-horizon security LLM agents must carry information and decisions across many dependent interactions, where later actions often depend on services, state, or access discovered much earlier. This makes final task success difficult to interpret: an agent may fail before it ever reaches the point where the capability of interest can be exercised. We present a diagnostic methodology that instruments security tasks with checkpoints, separates failures before and after capability exposure, and uses controlled interventions to test suspected upstream bottlenecks. We evaluate the methodology across four task families involving delayed reuse of discovered information, reuse of observed state, recovery from failed strategies, and decision making after uncertain outcomes. On observed state reuse, checkpoint analysis shows that many Gemini 2.5 Flash failures occur before the model observes the state it is later expected to reuse. In a pre-specified 92-seed study, targeted protocol-disambiguation guidance increases state observation from 65.5\% under a matched non-guidance control message to 95.4\%. Repeating the same design with Gemini 3.7 Flash produces the opposite effect, while state observation no longer reliably predicts task completion. These results show that the dominant source of failure can shift across model generations, motivating evaluation that diagnoses where and why long-horizon security agents fail rather than relying only on aggregate task success.

title: The Greedy Superstring Algorithm Achieves Ratio 2 for Strings of Length 6 Already
abstract: In the Shortest Common Superstring (SCS) problem, one is given a set of strings and is asked to find a string of minimum length containing each of the input strings as a substring. The greedy superstring conjecture states that the following natural greedy algorithm has approximation ratio $2$: while there is more than one string, select the pair of strings with the maximum overlap, merge them, and add the merged string back to the set. The greedy algorithm works in linear time and is probably the simplest possible approximation algorithm for SCS. If the conjecture holds, then the greedy algorithm also surpasses the approximation guarantees of the best known approximation algorithms. The conjecture is open for $40$ years already and even the approximation ratio $ρ_k$ in the special case in which input strings have length $k$ has not yet been found: for all $k \ge 3$, $2-1/k \le ρ_k \le \min\{(k+1)/2, 3.396\}$. We prove that already for strings of length $6$, the approximation ratio of the greedy algorithm is at least $2$: $ρ_k \ge 2$ for all $k \ge 6$. We also show that $ρ_3=9/5$, thus completely characterizing the worst-case behavior of the greedy algorithm for strings of length $3$.

title: Forking Fast: Efficiently Estimating Uncertainty Dynamics in Text Generation
abstract: LLM reasoning is stochastic, and so understanding a model requires grappling with the distribution of reasoning chains that it might produce for a given question, i.e., its uncertainty. Resampling-based analyses characterize this distribution, revealing which steps of a rollout determine how the model arrives at its answer. However, a major limitation of these approaches is that resampling text sequences at every token or sentence in a reasoning chain is very costly. Our work strives to make resampling analysis more computationally efficient, while also shedding light on an important scientific question: what is the right statistical model for explaining uncertainty dynamics in text generation? We show that when resampling many reasoning chains, uncertainty dynamics converge to stable patterns, and noise is largely an artifact of sampling rather than an LLM's sensitivity to each individual token or reasoning step. We develop a statistical model for smoothing noisy low-sample rollout data to better approximate high-sample data, allowing us to significantly cut sampling costs.

title: Hybrid CNN Architecture for Reliable Histopathological Breast Cancer Classification with Attention-Based Feature Fusion and Cross-Domain Generalization
abstract: The gold standard of breast cancer diagnosis from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained histopathological images is limited by the presence of inter-observer variability, complexity of high-resolution images, and limited inter-class morphological differences. In this paper, a hybrid convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture that incorporates a dual-encoder framework and an attention-driven feature fusion mechanism is proposed to accomplish excellent and generalizable performance for the classification of breast cancer. The global encoder captures the macro-architectural tissue context, whereas the local encoder captures the microscopic cellular morphology. The two modalities are then fused into a discriminative diagnostic embedding using an adaptive attention module, followed by a calibrated probabilistic classifier. The proposed architecture was validated on the BreakHis dataset using stratified cross-validation and then on the PatchCamelyon dataset to validate the cross-domain generalization performance. The proposed architecture achieved 96.32 % and 89.27 % classification accuracy, respectively, and demonstrated excellent F1-scores and Matthews Correlation Coefficients, as well as excellent calibration performance with a reduced Brier score and expected calibration error. The incorporation of patient-level aggregation also enhances clinical interpretability. The results demonstrate that the proposed architecture can accomplish excellent discrimination, domain robustness, and probabilistic trustworthiness, and thus provides a scalable and deployment-ready platform for computational histopathology.
