title: Learning Prostate Anatomy at Test Time for Cancer Detection in Micro-Ultrasound
abstract: Domain shift across clinical centers using different imaging hardware or acquisition protocols remains a fundamental barrier to deploying deep learning models for prostate cancer (PCa) detection. Existing test-time adaptation (TTA) methods address distribution shift through entropy minimization or augmentation-based self-supervision, correcting for statistical differences in image appearance but ignoring the anatomical structure of the target domain. We propose ANT, a segmentation-guided TTA framework that adapts a pretrained cancer detection encoder to the target domain by solving an auxiliary prostate segmentation task at test time, supervised by pseudo-masks from a frozen pretrained segmentation network. By aligning encoder representations to prostate anatomy in the target domain, ANT corrects domain-specific feature drift while preserving cancer-discriminative structure. The model was trained on 693 patients imaged with an earlier-generation micro-ultrasound scanner in a multi-center clinical trial, and evaluated on 118 patients acquired with a newer-generation system across two centers in another clinical trial. Under a leave-one-center-out protocol with identical evaluation conditions across all methods, ANT improves mean AUC by 2.9% and 3.6% at the biopsy-core and patient levels, respectively, over no adaptation, outperforming TTA baselines. Code is available at: https://github.com/ObedDzik/ant.git.

title: Contrastive Mixed Prompt Learning for Incomplete Multimodal Sentiment Analysis with Unseen Modality Combination
abstract: Incomplete multimodal sentiment analysis has garnered significant attention in recent years. Existing approaches typically assume that data is missing at random or are designed specifically for certain missing patterns, ignoring the modality combination inconsistency between training and testing phases. However, in real-world scenarios, the testing phase often encounters modal combinations that were not present during the training phase, which leads to insufficient generalization capabilities and unstable performance. In this paper, we introduce the problem of Incomplete Multimodal Sentiment Analysis with Unseen Modality Combinations (IMSAUMC), aiming to enhance model generalization for unseen modality combinations. To address this challenge, we propose the model named $\textbf{C}$ontrastive $\textbf{M}$ixed $\textbf{P}$rompt $\textbf{L}$earning ($\textsf{CMPL}$) for IMSAUMC. It introduces a label-guided contrastive feature learning mechanism to learn robust and discriminative cross-modal representations. Additionally, we design modality-combination prompts with a soft router to facilitate better learning of various modality combinations. Furthermore, we introduce three prompt contrastive learning strategies, which enable effective learning of prompts corresponding to unseen modality combinations, thereby significantly strengthening the model's generalization capabilities in diverse testing scenarios. Extensive experiments on three widely used datasets demonstrate that $\textsf{CMPL}$ achieves more than a 5% improvement in accuracy compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

title: Block3D: Efficient Text-to-3D Generation via Block-Wise Diffusion
abstract: While text-to-3D generation has advanced rapidly, achieving high geometric fidelity at low inference cost remains challenging. Existing text-to-3D methods either decode discrete shape tokens autoregressively or iteratively refine global 3D representations with diffusion or flow models. However, autoregressive decoding is sequential and cannot revise errors, whereas diffusion and flow-matching models repeatedly process the full representation, making high-quality generation increasingly expensive. In this paper, we propose Block3D, a block-wise diffusion framework that partitions the discrete shape-token sequence into contiguous blocks, generates the blocks autoregressively, and jointly denoises all tokens within the current block. To alleviate error accumulation, we introduce confidence-guided intra-block correction, which revises low-confidence tokens before each block is finalized. On a held-out set from TRELLIS-500K, Block3D reduces mean end-to-end generation time from 25.71 seconds to 4.99 seconds, achieving a 5.15times speedup over the fine-tuned autoregressive baseline without sacrificing geometric fidelity.

title: Tekoälyn hyödyntäminen yritysten CRM-järjestelmissä
abstract: Laajalti laskentatehon kasvun ja datan lisääntyneen määrän ansioista johtuneen tekoälyn kehittyminen on avannut uusia mahdollisuuksia yrityksille. Asiakassuhdehallinta ei ole tässä poikkeus ja tekoälyä on alettu implementoimaan myös asiakassuhdehallintajärjestelmiin. Asiakassuhdehallintajärjestelmiä käytetään tukena asiakkaiden hankinnassa ja arvonluomisessa. Ne yhdistävät yritysten kriittiset prosessit yhden järjestelmän alle ja luovat monipuolista hyötyä yrityksille riippuen haluamasta käyttötarkoituksesta. Perimmäinen tarkoitus on tyydyttää asiakkaiden tarpeet. Tekoälyn rooli CRM-järjestelmissä on datan analysointi ja erilaisten prosessien automatisointi. Tekoäly tukee yritysten asiakassuhteiden ylläpitoa ja asiakasvalinnan prosessia. Se luo laajemman ja tarkemman kuvan mah-dollisista ja nykyisistä asiakkaista. Laajemmalla tiedolla pystytään luomaan paremmin arvoa asiakkaille esi-merkiksi persoonallisemmalla palvelulla ja markkinoinnilla. Tekoälyn avulla voidaan myös ennustaa tulevai-suuden trendejä. Automatisoimalla rutiininomaisia prosesseja yritys pystyy vapauttamaan ja kohdistamaan ra-jalliset resurssinsa tarkemmin. Nämä kaikki ohjaavat yrityksen strategisia toimenpiteitä. Tutkielma kertoo monipuolisesti tekoälyn tuomista hyödyistä CRM-järjestelmissä. Tutkielma käsittelee myös tekoälyn integroinnista aiheutuvia haasteita ja haittoja, sekä pyrkii antamaan mahdollisia ratkaisuja näihin haasteisiin. Tutkielma käsittelee myös yleisesti tekoälyn toimintaa ja sen eri malleja. Tutkielmassa on käytetty lähteinä pääsääntöisesti lähivuosina tehtyjä tutkimuksia. Tutkielmassa ei syvennytä pitkälle tekniseen puoleen, vaan pyritään antamaan yleinen käsitys tekoälyn hyödyntämisestä asiakassuhde-hallinnassa. Tavoitteena on antaa lukijalle käsitys siitä, mitä tekoälyn implementointi CRM-järjestelmiin vaatii ja mitä hyötyjä se mahdollisesti tuo.

title: Dataset of Random Byte Strings for Label Private Set Intersection
abstract: This dataset comprises a collection of random byte-string datasets designed specifically for testing Label Private Set Intersection (LPSI) protocols. It includes both server-side and client-side data. Taking the file s16-8.csv as an example, this file denotes the server-side dataset with a server set size of 2^{16} and a client set size of 2^{8}. Each record in the server dataset consists of a 64-byte random string (data item) and a 6-byte random string (label item). The corresponding client-side dataset is provided in the file c16-8.csv.The datasets are generated using Python scripts that produce random byte strings. This dataset is intended solely for performance evaluation of LPSI protocols and is not associated with any specific application scenario. All data are synthetically generated random bytes and do not originate from any real-world environment or actual operational data.

title: Replication package for capability and deployability of compact language models for governed tool calling
abstract: Code, configuration, frozen API-Bank evaluation inventory, item-level observations, statistical analyses, and deterministic table/figure generators supporting the study Capability and deployability of compact language models for governed tool calling in intelligent information systems. The package contains the 292-observation four-model paired main run and the 584-observation prompt/schema ablation. Model weights and manuscript files are not included.

title: Computational Boundary Minimality
abstract: This paper investigates the concept of computational boundary minimality, focusing on identifying the smallest boundary, denoted as [B*(C)], that satisfies a specific condition: [C C1|B*|C2]. The core argument posits that any modification to this boundary, represented as [B*-{b}], will lead to a change in the probability distribution, P(C). The paper formally establishes that [B*(C)] represents the minimal computational boundary, encapsulated within a box. The primary goal is to provide a foundational understanding of this concept and its implications within computational modelling and data analysis, without engaging in experimental validation.

title: Data for a publication - Sensitivity-Based Robustness Evaluation of a Reinforcement Learning Controller for the Furuta Pendulum under Parametric Uncertainty †
abstract: This paper presents a sensitivity analysis of a reinforcement learning (RL) controller for stabilization of the Furuta pendulum under parameter variations. A high-fidelity multibody model of the system is first developed in Adams and used for policy training and closed-loop assessment. The RL agent is trained on the nominal model to stabilize the pendulum about the upright equilibrium. The trained policy is then evaluated by independently perturbing selected physical parameters within prescribed intervals around their nominal values. The resulting responses are used to assess the sensitivity of the learned policy to parameter variations. A trial is classified as failed when either the pendulum angle or the rotary arm exceeds its prescribed limit. The analysis identifies the parameters that have the greatest influence on policy performance and estimates the parameter ranges over which the trained policy continues to stabilize the pendulum. These results provide insight into the sensitivity of the trained policy to modelling errors and physical parameter variations.

title: Information Irreducible Core
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework, termed "Information Irreducible Core" (IIC), centered on the concept that all complex knowledge systems possess a fundamentally uncompressable core. This core, analogous to prime numbers in mathematics, represents the irreducible essence of the information. The framework introduces "Information Core Decomposition" (ICD), a methodology for identifying and characterizing these irreducible components within various domains of knowledge. The analysis leverages the principles of information theory, specifically entropy and redundancy, to differentiate between reducible and irreducible information. The core argument posits that while information can be represented and processed through various levels of abstraction and compression, a certain level of intrinsic complexity will always remain, representing the foundational, unyielding information. The paper will explore the implications of this concept across diverse fields, including data science, cognitive science, and knowledge representation, and provides a theoretical foundation for understanding the limits and nature of knowledge reduction. The ultimate goal is to move beyond a purely reductive approach to knowledge, acknowledging the inherent irreducible components that define its fundamental structure.

title: Multi-Modal Deep Learning Framework for Prediction and Early Identification of Neoplasms: A Hybrid CNN-Transformer Architecture with Explainability
abstract: Early and accurate detection of neoplasms is a critical challenge in clinical oncology, where diagnostic delays substantially reduce patient survival rates.This paper proposes a novel Multi-Modal Hybrid CNN-Transformer (MMHCT) framework for simultaneous early prediction and identification of neoplasms across five cancer types: breast, lung, brain, prostate, and colorectal.The architecture fuses spatial feature extraction via a modified ResNet-50 backbone with long-range dependency modeling through a Vision Transformer (ViT-B/16) encoder.A Cross-Modal Attention Fusion (CMAF) mechanism integrates heterogeneous inputs, including CT, MRI, whole-slide histopathology images, and structured Electronic Health Records (EHR).A custom focal Dice loss function and federated learning protocol address class imbalance and data privacy constraints, respectively.On the TCGA-LUAD, CBIS-DDSM, BraTS-2023, and Patch Camelyon benchmarks, MMHCT achieves mean AUC = 0.974, sensitivity = 94.3%, specificity = 96.1%,and F1-score = 0.943 at stage-I detection, outperforming all nine baseline methods.GRAD-CAM++ saliency maps and SHAP feature attributions are embedded to ensure clinical interpretability.The framework complies with GDPR and HIPAA regulations through differential privacy mechanisms with privacy budget epsilon = 0.3.

title: Learning Adaptive Cross-Modal Interactions for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
abstract: Multimodal sentiment analysis aims to integrate heterogeneous textual, visual, and acoustic information for effective emotion understanding. However, existing methods often suffer from insufficient cross-modal interaction modeling, limited adaptability in multimodal fusion, and inadequate suppression of modality-specific noise under complex conversational scenarios. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a framework for learning adaptive cross-modal interactions for multimodal sentiment analysis. The proposed framework consists of three stages: modality-aware preprocessing, heterogeneous representation learning, and adaptive multimodal fusion. First, a unified preprocessing strategy is designed to improve cross-modal consistency through textual normalization, speaker-aware visual alignment, and utterance-level acoustic representation enhancement. Second, modality-specific encoders are constructed to capture complementary semantic, spatial, and utterance-level acoustic characteristics from textual, visual, and acoustic modalities, respectively. Third, an adaptive fusion framework is introduced to explicitly model cross-modal interactions, dynamically estimate the importance of different modality combinations, and further calibrate discriminative feature channels through channel attention. By jointly performing modality-level interaction learning and channel-wise feature refinement, the proposed framework effectively enhances multimodal representation capability for sentiment classification. Extensive experiments conducted on the CMU-MOSI and MELD benchmark datasets demonstrate that our framework consistently outperforms previous methods. In particular, the proposed model achieves 90.27% accuracy and 90.26% F1-score on CMU-MOSI, together with 66.57% accuracy and 66.21% F1-score on MELD. Additional ablation studies and qualitative analyses further validate the effectiveness of the proposed preprocessing strategy, modality-specific representation learning, and adaptive fusion mechanism.

title: Ethical Implications of Prompt Injection in AI-mediated Grading: An Adversarial Red-Team Evaluation
abstract: Abstract The increasing integration of AI tools into academic work introduces both opportunities and new security risks, particularly concerning the integrity of evaluative practices. This study investigates the robustness of AI‑mediated work in higher education by examining whether indirect prompt injection attacks can manipulate course assessment outcomes. The aim is to examine how vulnerable AI‑supported grading processes are to hidden adversarial inputs and to explore potential implications for academic trust, fairness, and integrity in AI-mediated assessment. The study applies a structured adversarial security evaluation, drawing on red‑team testing methodologies. A synthetic student submission was generated and paired with five different indirect prompt injection attempts using combinations of different adversarial prompt techniques. Each attempt was iterated multiple times across different file formats against the same AI tool (Microsoft Copilot) under realistic usage conditions. The results show that several prompt injection attempts successfully altered the output, with some attack strategies achieving success rates between 94 and 100%, while remaining undetected in the output. These findings highlight a discrepancy between security safeguards and system behaviour, raising concerns for AI‑mediated academic work. The study argues for development of clear guidelines and policies for AI use, improved professional development, and standardised assessments for prompt injection resilience in organisations.

title: An Inclusive and Lightweight Approach to Federated Continual Learning for Cultural Heritage
abstract: Artificial intelligence can support cultural heritage and digital humanities through large-scale retrieval and analysis of digitized collections. However, cultural heritage data are often distributed across institutions, constrained by ownership and access restrictions, and continuously evolving over time. Federated Continual Learning (FCL) is well suited to this setting, as it enables models to learn from distributed and sequential data without sharing raw collections. In this paper, we propose FedCurv-DR, a lightweight, regularisation-based FCL strategy. The method accumulates parameter-importance estimates across clients and experiences to protect learned knowledge, while updating them only at fixed intervals to minimize communication and computation overhead. We evaluate FedCurv-DR in a continual learning scenario using the WikiArt image dataset for genre classification with evolving styles, reporting performance, energy, and fairness metrics. Our results show that FedCurv- DR reduces forgetting and balances performance, fairness, and energy efficiency for sustainable AI in cultural heritage.

title: The Forward-Backward Disconnect: State Dynamics, Credit Assignment, and Biological Grounding in Neural Computation
abstract: A recurring pattern in neural computation is the reintroduction of dynamical and biological structure into models originally simplified for scalable optimization. Early feedforward networks reduced biological neurons to threshold or rate-like summation units, an abstraction compatible with global-gradient training at scale. Since then, forward computation has diversified: modern architectures carry recurrent state, retrieve from long contexts through attention and associative memory, compress histories through structured state-space dynamics, evolve in continuous time, settle to implicit equilibria, and communicate through sparse spikes. Training has diversified less. Scalable learning remains concentrated around backpropagation, backpropagation through time, adjoint methods, implicit differentiation, and surrogate-gradient variants. We call this asymmetry the forward-backward disconnect and develop a taxonomy spanning neural model families along three coupled axes: state-dynamics structure, credit-assignment mechanism, and biological grounding. Forward and learning grounding are treated separately, and the unit of analysis is the architecture-learning configuration rather than the architecture name alone. Across static, recurrent, attention-based, state-space, continuous-time, implicit, spiking, biologically plausible, and neuromorphic families, forward dynamics have diversified while the highest demonstrated scales remain concentrated in global or closely gradient-derived error-propagation mechanisms. Closing this disconnect requires better alignment among state dynamics, credit assignment, and computational substrate.

title: Reliable Financial Named Entity Recognition Under Domain Shift: Confidence Estimation and Selective Prediction
abstract: Financial AI systems often train information extractors on one textual register and deploy them across filings, news, and user-generated content, and standard F1 scores do not indicate which predictions remain safe to automate when that input distribution changes. We study confidence estimation and selective prediction for financial named entity recognition (NER) on a three-tier stress test spanning SEC filings, financial news, and general-topic social media as an extreme out-of-domain condition, evaluating a BERT tagger and LoRA-tuned Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B models with five inference-time confidence signals, three training seeds, and bootstrap intervals. Confidence rankings themselves change under shift: whole-output probability is the strongest in-domain error detector but deteriorates out of domain, whereas entity-span probability and self-consistency are more robust; self-consistency is also better calibrated without post-hoc fitting. Abstention reduces sentence error from 34.3% to below 2% on the highest-confidence 40% of in-domain inputs and remains useful on financial news, but recovers no usefully large clean subset under the extreme social-media shift. These results motivate a staged deployment strategy that detects severe distribution shift upstream before applying prediction-level confidence gating.

title: Stream4D: 4D-Consistency for Streaming Autoregressive Diffusion Video Models
abstract: Streaming autoregressive diffusion models enable real-time, long-horizon video generation, but their training objectives optimize local frame prediction rather than the geometry and dynamics of a coherent world: long rollouts accumulate geometric drift and degrade into static or unnatural motion. Recent bidirectional approaches address this problem using rewards signals built upon 3D Gaussian-Splatting reconstruction. However, a single rigid 3d reconstruction cannot model a dynamic scene, so this critic penalizes genuine object motion as reconstruction error and is maximized by freezing the video. This shortcut is especially detrimental in the AR setting, where each chunk can propagate an already-static configuration. In this work, we propose Stream4D, which replaces the static critic with a feed-forward 4D reconstruction reward that explicitly models scene dynamics, allowing coherent motion to receive high consistency rewards. To further guide motion magnitude and quality, we add a motion prior that rewards natural scene-flow magnitude while penalizing jitter and non-rigid artifacts. Our final recipe combines these two terms with a lightweight perceptual anchor. Across various autoregressive video backbones and various generation horizons, Stream4D improves 4D reconstruction quality, preserves motion more effectively, and achieves higher human-aligned preference. Project page: https://banyuanhao.github.io/Stream4D/

title: Simulasi Sistem Kendali Adaptif Menggunakan Fuzzy-PID pada Pengatur Ketinggian Drone
abstract: Pengendalian ketinggian (altitude control) merupakan aspek penting dalam menjaga kestabilan penerbangan quadcopter. Salah satu metode yang umum digunakan adalah PID controller, yang performanya sangat dipengaruhi oleh ketepatan parameter Kp, Ki, dan Kd. Penelitian ini mengusulkan metode auto-tuning PID berbasis logika fuzzy Mamdani untuk mengendalikan ketinggian quadcopter secara otomatis. Berdasarkan simulasi dua dimensi, sistem hanya mencapai kestabilan pada periode pembaharuan parameter tinggi (nilai 2000 dan 3000) dengan waktu 21-22 detik. Nilai Kp awal menjadi faktor paling dominan, di mana Kp = 1 berhasil stabil, sedangkan Kp = 10 gagal. Di sisi lain, sistem terbukti adaptif terhadap gangguan mekanis karena mampu kembali stabil saat massa drone berubah dengan pemulihan 2-17 detik. Kesimpulannya, metode ini stabil dan adaptif, namun sangat sensitif terhadap kondisi awal periode pembaharuan dan nilai Kp.

title: Proof Phase Transition
abstract: The concept of a phase transition is well established in statistical physics, where a small change in an external parameter can lead to a dramatic shift in macroscopic behavior. In this paper we extend the notion of phase transition to the realm of formal proofs. We formalize a proof system as a graph whose vertices are intermediate deduction steps and whose edges represent inference rules. By introducing a new hypothesis into the proof environment we observe that the space of possible proofs undergoes a qualitative change: a previously impossible proof becomes tractable, and the complexity of the proof search drops from exponential to polynomial. We define the notion of a Proof Critical Point, the parameter value at which this transition occurs, and we prove that the proof space possesses a well-defined phase diagram analogous to that in physical systems. The results suggest that proof complexity is governed by underlying combinatorial structures that can be manipulated by targeted hypothesis augmentation. Keywords: Proof Complexity, Phase Transition, Critical Point, Proof Graph, Deductive Reasoning.

title: Algorithmic Conservation Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Algorithmic Conservation Theory, a novel framework examining algorithms beyond their traditional complexity analysis. It posits that algorithms possess inherent "algorithmic invariants" – structural properties that, once established, remain constant throughout their execution. These invariants are not simply side effects but represent fundamental characteristics of the algorithm's state and operation. The theory further proposes the existence of "conservation transforms" – transformations between algorithms that preserve these invariants. This approach offers a deeper understanding of algorithmic behavior, potentially leading to new optimization strategies and a more rigorous evaluation of algorithmic efficiency. The core of the theory rests on the formal definition of algorithmic invariants and the identification of conservation transforms, providing a foundational structure for future algorithmic research.

title: Algorithmic Interference Cancellation
abstract: This paper explores the theoretical framework of algorithmic interference cancellation, focusing on the design of a universal operation capable of mitigating interference between two computational processes. The core concept revolves around a function, denoted as *C(A,B)*, which, when applied to a computational process *A* and a related process *B*, aims to approximate the interference term *I(A,C(A,B))* to zero. The investigation delves into identifying general conditions under which such a function can be constructed, potentially leading to new developments in program combination theory. The paper outlines the fundamental definitions, explores the theoretical challenges, and discusses the implications of successful interference cancellation for complex computational systems. The focus remains on the theoretical aspects without empirical validation or experimental results. ---

title: Information Conservation of Structure
abstract: This paper explores the concept of information conservation within structural transformations. It posits that while the content of information can undergo modification during a conversion process, the underlying structural information remains fundamentally preserved. This preservation is characterized by the quantity of Structural Information Quantity (SIQ), which serves as a metric for assessing the degree of structural integrity maintained throughout the transformation. The paper outlines a theoretical framework for understanding this phenomenon, emphasizing the importance of structural elements in determining the resilience and interpretability of information systems. The core argument is that certain structural properties act as anchors, preventing complete disintegration of information even when the specific details are altered. This work lays the groundwork for further research into the implications of this principle across various domains, including data compression, knowledge representation, and information retrieval.

title: Computational Freedom Theory
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Freedom Theory (CFT), a novel framework for understanding and evaluating system capabilities beyond traditional metrics such as parameter count. CFT posits that a system's ability is fundamentally determined by its 'Computational Freedom Dimension' (CFD), which is directly proportional to the number of available computational freedoms. This theory challenges the conventional assumption that increasing parameters automatically equates to increased system capability. The core argument is that the *strategic* utilization of these parameters – the freedom to manipulate and transform them – is the key determinant of performance. The theory is presented with a formal definition of CFD and explores its implications for various system domains. The research outlines a methodology for assessing CFD, emphasizing the importance of considering not just the quantity of parameters but also the potential for computational manipulation and the resulting impact on system behavior. This work aims to shift the focus from mere parameterization to a more nuanced understanding of system intelligence and adaptability.

title: Universal Program Decomposition (UPD) Theory
abstract: This paper introduces the Universal Program Decomposition (UPD) theory, a novel approach to software design and analysis. The core premise of UPD is that any complex program possesses a unique and optimal decomposition, fundamentally different from traditional modularization techniques. Instead of relying on functional or data-flow based decomposition, UPD postulates a mathematical uniqueness in the optimal decomposition, representing a single, definitive solution. This theory is presented with a formal framework, including the core axioms and operational definitions. The paper outlines the key concepts, provides a detailed explanation of the decomposition process, and establishes the conditions under which the unique optimal decomposition can be identified. The theory is presented with a focus on mathematical rigor and aims to shift the paradigm in software engineering towards a more precise and verifiable approach to program design. The decomposition process is described as a transformation that maps a complex program to a set of primitive operations, adhering to strict mathematical constraints. The ultimate goal is to enable automated program analysis and verification based on this mathematically defined decomposition.

title: Computational Habitat Evolution
abstract: This paper explores a novel algorithmic approach to evolutionary research, termed Computational Habitat Evolution (CHE). Instead of relying on traditional methods of data selection and analysis, CHE focuses on the continuous creation and refinement of simulated environments, allowing algorithms to evolve directly within these dynamically generated habitats. The core principle is that the algorithm's evolution is intrinsically linked to the properties of its surrounding environment. This paper details the conceptual framework, outlines the key algorithmic components, and presents a theoretical model for understanding this co-evolutionary process. The central equation governing this process is: ΔH/Δt = α * (∂E/∂H) + β * (∂E/∂A) Where: * ΔH/Δt represents the rate of change in the habitat (H). * α is a parameter reflecting the influence of environmental factors on the algorithm's evolution. * ∂E/∂H represents the gradient of the fitness function (E) with respect to the habitat characteristics (H). * β is a parameter reflecting the algorithm's influence on the environment. * ∂E/∂A represents the gradient of the fitness function with respect to the algorithm's actions (A). The paper argues that this approach offers a more realistic and potentially more efficient method for studying evolutionary processes, particularly in complex and uncertain environments. Further exploration of the parameters α and β, and the design of diverse habitat creation mechanisms, are identified as key areas for future research.

title: Lung Cancer Classification from Chest CT Scans Using EfficientNet
abstract: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths, and early detection is critical for improving survival.This study presents an explainable deep learning approach for classifying chest CT scans into normal, benign, and malignant categories.Six pretrained convolutional neural networks were evaluated on the public IQ-OTH/NCCD dataset using class-weighted training and light data augmentation.EfficientNet-B0 achieved the best performance, with 99.39% accuracy, a 0.988 macro F1score, and 0.996 AUC, while correctly identifying all malignant cases.

title: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) for Predictive Analytics in Tourism Marketing
abstract: AI and ML is transforming tourism marketing by helping destinations predict visitor behaviour, personalize campaigns, and increase revenue. This research examines the use of AI predictive analytics in tourism, focusing on India and nearby regions. Using a mixed-methods study, data was collected from tourism professionals, travellers, and experts. The study found AI algorithms could predict tourist preferences with nearly 80% accuracy. Using chatbots and influencers boosted engagement the most, by 41.2% and 36.5% respectively, while AI revenue strategies raised overall earnings by 12.8%—hotels saw a 14.2% increase. However, major ethical concerns were noted, primarily data privacy (68.5%), lack of transparency (59.7%), and algorithmic bias (52.3%). These findings emphasize the necessity for ethical AI frameworks to promote responsible and sustainable utilization of these technologies. This study offers actionable insights for tourism marketers and enriches the ongoing academic conversation on AI's role in tourism.

title: When Graph-JEPA Learns the Wrong Thing: Diagnosing and Repairing Category-Conditional Collapse
abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures are selected almost universally by linear probing and effective rank. We report a case where both read healthily while the representation carries zero usable instance information. We repair it, and a second failure appears: the repaired metric saturates on a target carrying no structural information. Our corpus is a scientific-reasoning graph over 57,903 articles, each a subgraph. A Graph-JEPA predicts one masked aspect from a subgraph's remaining aspects, attaining linear-probe accuracy 0.871 and effective rank 18-47, yet retrieval recovers 0.00 of 14.4 bits (MRR 1.9e-4 vs chance 1.99e-4, p=0.98). Three upper bounds on the same pool and code recover nearly everything (+14.28, +14.34, +14.22 bits), ruling out corpus, masking, pool, and metric as causes. We trace this to variance allocation - frozen inputs place 86.05% of variance on subgraph identity and 0.40% on aspect identity, while trained latents place 0.39% and 99.61%. This is a property of the objective's optimum: the degenerate solution is a global minimum of the coupled predictor/EMA-target objective, present already at init. A repaired configuration reaches 14.377 of 14.379 bits, above the 13.865-bit oracle; reverting the loss to regression drops it to 0.307 bits, confirming it. Yet the repair licenses nothing about reasoning: the target is reducible, since intra-subgraph edges are a deterministic function of node census. The oracle reaches 96.4% of the ceiling, and our largest effect is the learning-rate schedule, not architecture. Bits and a reasoning probe show no relation across ten cells. A data-derived target fails a quality gate - 25.96% of nodes are duplicate placeholders, and the rest is more generic than supporting evidence. Rank, probes, and metrics can all saturate on an unsupportive evaluation. We release a harness with a reducibility audit and target gate.

title: Evaluasi Kinerja Algoritma Kriptografi Lightweight Pada File Suara Jantung di Perangkat IoT Sebagai Simulasi Pengamanan Data Medis Digital
abstract: Perkembangan Internet of Things (IoT) dalam bidang kesehatan mendorong kebutuhan pengamanan data medis digital yang diproses pada perangkat embedded. Salah satu bentuk data medis digital yang dapat diproses adalah file suara jantung atau phonocardiogram dalam format WAV. Penelitian ini bertujuan mengevaluasi kinerja algoritma AES-128 dan SPECK pada file suara jantung di perangkat IoT berbasis ESP32 sebagai simulasi pengamanan data medis digital. Data uji berupa 15 file WAV dari PhysioNet/Computing in Cardiology Challenge 2016 yang dibagi menjadi kategori kecil, sedang, dan besar. Setiap file diuji lima kali sehingga diperoleh 75 data pengujian. Waktu yang diukur hanya mencakup eksekusi algoritma pada data yang telah dibaca ke buffer, tanpa menghitung pembacaan SD card, tampilan LCD, delay LED, dan keluaran Serial Monitor. Hasil pengujian menunjukkan seluruh proses dekripsi AES-128 dan SPECK berhasil mengembalikan data sesuai data asli. Rata-rata waktu enkripsi AES-128 adalah 45.551,87 µs, sedangkan SPECK 38.048,47 µs. Rata-rata waktu dekripsi AES-128 adalah 46.906,40 µs, sedangkan SPECK 45.635,16 µs. SPECK lebih cepat 16,46% pada enkripsi dan 2,68% pada dekripsi. Throughput enkripsi SPECK mencapai 2.386,19 KB/s, lebih tinggi dari AES-128 sebesar 1.993,40 KB/s. Program menggunakan 375.186 byte program storage dan 24.360 byte dynamic memory. Hasil statistik ciphertext menunjukkan entropy mendekati 8, correlation mendekati 0, histogram CV relatif kecil, dan chi-square mendekati distribusi seragam. Dengan demikian, SPECK lebih efisien dibandingkan AES-128 pada skenario pengujian file suara jantung di ESP32, tetapi hasil ini tidak digeneralisasikan secara mutlak untuk seluruh jenis data dan seluruh perangkat.

title: Algorithmic Realization Bottleneck
abstract: This paper investigates the concept of an "algorithmic realization bottleneck," a critical limitation encountered during algorithmic transformations. The core idea posits that a transformation from state *P* to state *Q* necessitates a specific structural component, denoted as *B*, to be traversed. If all paths between *P* and *Q* are constrained to pass through *B*, then *B* is defined as the realization bottleneck. This seemingly simple definition leads to a profound consequence: the potential for formulating impossibility theorems within algorithmic transformation contexts. The paper explores the implications of this bottleneck, focusing on the conditions under which it arises and the resulting limitations on the feasibility of certain algorithmic changes. The analysis presented here provides a foundational understanding of this bottleneck and highlights its potential role in shaping the boundaries of algorithmic design and transformation. The focus is on the theoretical framework and conceptual exploration, without empirical experimentation. ---

title: Algorithmic Order Entropy
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Algorithmic Order Entropy (H\_O), a novel metric designed to quantify the degree of constraint imposed upon a solution process by an algorithm. H\_O measures the probability distribution of all possible valid solution sequences (denoted as π) within a given problem space and then calculates the entropy of this distribution. High entropy values indicate a high degree of freedom in the solution process, suggesting an algorithm that allows for diverse and potentially creative approaches. Conversely, low entropy values signify a strong bias towards specific solution sequences, implying that the algorithm effectively dictates the order in which the problem is tackled. The paper provides a formal definition of H\_O, establishes its relationship to probability distributions, and explores its implications for understanding and evaluating algorithmic design. The core idea is to shift the focus from simply measuring the efficiency of an algorithm to assessing the level of imposed structure—a structure that can, in certain contexts, be detrimental to optimal or innovative solutions. This work lays the foundation for further research into the design of algorithms that promote exploration and flexibility, rather than rigid, deterministic pathways.

title: Universal Context Calculus
abstract: This paper introduces the Universal Context Calculus (UCC), a novel approach to formalizing computation that moves beyond the traditional program-plus-input model. UCC posits that modern computation, particularly as exemplified by Large Language Models (LLMs) and agents, fundamentally involves the interaction of a program, input, and, crucially, context. The calculus itself is designed to handle the complex operations associated with context: combination, transformation, inheritance, isolation, pollution, equivalence, and elimination. The core argument is that traditional program semantics represent a specific case of UCC, allowing for a unified description of diverse computational systems. This paper outlines the foundational concepts of UCC and highlights its potential to bridge the gap between established programming theory and the rapidly evolving landscape of modern AI and distributed systems. We explore the key advantages of UCC and position it as a promising area for long-term research.

title: Awareness and Adoption of AI-Powered Chatbots among Student Entrepreneurs in Lagos State University, Nigeria
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI)-powered chatbots become increasingly cost-effective and adaptable tools for handling customer interactions, student entrepreneurs are recognising their potential in marketing, brand communication, and operational efficiency. Despite this growing interest, little research has explored the awareness and adoption patterns of chatbots among studentpreneurs . This chapter investigates the level of awareness and factors influencing chatbot adoption among students at Lagos State University, using the Technology Acceptance Model as its theoretical foundation. This study adopts a qualitative approach using two focused group discussions with 17 studentpreneurs and 20 student customers drawn from four faculties within the university. The findings revealed a high level of awareness, with adoption largely driven by perceived usefulness, peer influence, and exposure through social media. Many studentpreneurs use chatbots for content creation, brand promotion, and customer engagement. However, concerns were raised about the generic nature of chatbot responses, reliability issues, and the lack of emotional nuance in interactions. These limitations suggest a need for improved personalisation and strategic training. This study recommends integrating chatbot literacy into entrepreneurship programmes across Nigerian universities and promoting the inclusion of AI in small-scale business practices. This will help unlock the full potential of chatbots as tools for innovation and growth in student-led enterprises.

title: Teaching Language Models to Reason: Self-Supervision and Intrinsic Structure
abstract: Training language models to reason effectively typically requires extensive human supervision in the form of labeled final answers or annotated reasoning traces. This dependence limits scalability and also does not ensure models exhibit a sound reasoning process without exploiting spurious shortcuts. This thesis explores strategies to improve reasoning in language models through self-supervision, and identifies structural properties of the reasoning process that are predictive of strong generalization. First, the thesis develops self-supervised training methods that enable models to generate robust training signals grounded in their own reasoning processes. I show that consensus across multiple sampled solutions can replace gold labels for preference optimization, and that models can be trained to produce execution-grounded feedback in the form of discriminative unit tests for code tasks. Iterative self-training with these signals enables smaller models to rival or outperform much larger systems on mathematical and logical reasoning, as well as code generation. The thesis additionally explores complementary inference-time strategies where models adaptively decompose tasks, discover reusable abstractions, and reformulate multimodal inputs to improve performance on downstream reasoning tasks without parameter updates. Second, the thesis moves beyond optimizing solely for correctness and investigates the structural properties of reasoning that make it effective. I develop reference-free evaluation methods that assess the content of reasoning chains -- their coherence, informativeness, and progress toward the final answer. I then connect reasoning effectiveness to the compressibility of the task's loss landscape through intrinsic dimensionality, a measure of the degrees of freedom needed to encode the task. I establish that effective reasoning chains reduce this intrinsic dimensionality, and that this compressibility is predictive of generalization. Together, these works outline a path toward reasoning systems that autonomously improve through self-supervision, and lay groundwork for future methods that leverage structural insights to guide the improvement process itself.

title: Stability-based partitions for ensemble clustering
abstract: Unsupervised clustering is challenging because there is no gold standard, making cluster quality assessment difficult. Clustering solutions depend on several choices the investigator makes, including the algorithm, hyperparameters, measures of dissimilarity, and the number of clusters. Stability has become a valuable tool for characterizing the quality of a clustering solution and prioritizing clusters. This work presents Stability-based Partitions for Ensemble Clustering (SPEC) to combine partitions from different clustering solutions to produce aggregate clustering. SPEC utilizes a graph-based representation of partitions with edge weights calculated from normalized item-level subsampled stability within a partition. Community detection with weighted bipartite graphs identifies the aggregate clusters within the graph. SPEC can aggregate solutions within a clustering algorithm with different hyperparameters across different clustering algorithms and integrate multi-modal data. SPEC applications to simulation and real data reveal that the stability-weighted graph is robust to noise and spurious solutions and can emphasize different geometries in the feature space. Applications to a METABRIC (Molecular Taxonomy of Breast Cancer International Consortium) dataset show that SPEC combined clinic data, gene expression data, and genetic mutation data to identify subpopulations of patients with differential survival profiles.

title: Binary Dhole Optimization Algorithm with bell-shaped transfer function for feature selection
abstract: This research introduces the Binary Dhole Optimization Algorithm (BDOA), a novel binary optimization method for feature selection problems inspired by the cooperative hunting behavior of dholes. Feature selection is an important task in machine learning because it can reduce computational cost, improve classification performance, and eliminate irrelevant and redundant features. However, selecting an optimal subset of features remains a challenging combinatorial optimization problem, especially for high-dimensional datasets. To address this issue, this study extends the original Dhole Optimization Algorithm into the binary domain through the use of novel Bell-shaped transfer functions. These transfer functions map continuous search dynamics into binary decisions while maintaining a balance between exploration and exploitation. Unlike traditional transfer functions, the proposed Bell-shaped transfer functions help reduce excessive bit flipping, preserve population diversity, and avoid premature convergence. The proposed BDOA was evaluated using multiple benchmark datasets and compared with several well-known binary optimization algorithms. The experimental results show that BDOA achieved competitive classification accuracy, lower fitness values, and fewer selected features across different datasets. In particular, BDOA achieved strong performance on datasets such as Ionosphere, Breast Cancer WD, Iris, Lung Cancer, and Human Activity Recognition. The results demonstrate that the proposed Bell-shaped transfer functions improve convergence behavior, computational efficiency, and solution quality. Quantitatively, BDOA improved the average classification accuracy from 0.8282 for the original DOA to 0.8718, representing an absolute improvement of 4.36% points. In terms of mean fitness value, BDOA achieved the lowest average value of 0.0786 across all datasets, compared with 0.0896 for the closest competing method, representing an absolute reduction of 0.0110. Therefore, BDOA can be considered an effective and robust approach for binary optimization and feature selection problems. The source code of the proposed BDOA is publicly available at: https://github.com/bnyad95/Binary-Dhole-Optimization-Algorithm-BDOA .

title: Clifford-efficient sparse state preparation for molecular wavefunctions
abstract: Sparse quantum state preparation concerns an $n$-qubit target state that is a superposition of only $d \ll 2^n$ computational basis states. Existing approaches exploit this sparsity by compressing these $d$ basis states and their amplitudes onto a smaller set of qubits, called the dense register, before expanding the prepared state to the full register. Rather than relying on the permutation-based compression used in prior work, we exploit affine relationships among the binary configurations over the finite field $\operatorname{GF}(2)$ to reduce both the non-Clifford gate count and the ancillary qubit count. Invertible affine transformations over $\operatorname{GF}(2)$, comprising Gaussian elimination and all-ones-row removal, first reduce the dense register from $n$ to the rank $r$ using only Clifford gates and no ancillary qubits. An optional binary encoding stage then trades additional Toffoli gates and ancillary qubits for further compression to the minimum $\lceil\log_2 d\rceil$ dense qubits needed to represent $d$ distinct configurations. For chemically relevant wavefunctions, such as those obtained from selected configuration interaction calculations, shared electronic excitation patterns produce many of these affine relationships, enabling substantial Clifford-only compression before binary encoding. Across the molecular benchmarks, our method requires the fewest ancillary qubits among the evaluated sparse state preparation methods while maintaining comparable non-Clifford gate counts when using binary encoding.

title: Beyond Memory Majority: Latent-Source Reasoning for Multi-Agent Memory Arbitration
abstract: Long-term multi-agent systems continuously accumulate the memories produced by different agents. Existing memory methods typically treat retrieved memories as independent evidence and combine them through voting or weighting. However, this independence assumption often fails in multi-agent settings: memories written by different agents may inherit the same upstream source or shared bias, causing correlated evidence to be repeatedly counted and creating a false majority. We term this failure mode \textit{Memory Correlation Bias}. To address the issue, we propose the \textbf{C}orrelation-\textbf{A}ware \textbf{M}emory \textbf{A}rbitration (CAMA) framework that jointly decouples retrieved memories and recovers missing independent evidence. We model the retrieved memories as query-conditioned evidence groups and combine neural dependency inference with provenance-based symbolic priors to estimate the effective number of independent evidence sources, thereby preventing correlated memories from forming a false majority. Since critical independent evidence may be absent from the initial retrieval set, \textsc{CAMA} further learns a sequential recovery policy that actively retrieves alternative evidence or traces upstream sources before making the final decision, aiming to recover sufficient independent evidence for reliable arbitration while minimizing retrieval cost. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our method over the state-of-the-art baseline methods, suppressing false majorities induced by correlated memories.

title: Does Listening Matter? Backchanneling and Nodding in AI Clone
abstract: AI clones that imitate a specific person typically reproduce what the person says and how they sound, but not how they listen. We investigate whether adding multimodal listening behaviors gives such a clone more presence and authenticity. We integrated verbal backchannels and head nodding, driven by real-time prediction models, into an AI clone equipped with voice cloning and LLM-based responses. In a within-subjects study (N=35), adding these behaviors significantly improved the perceived attentiveness of the avatar, the sense of talking with the real person, and the feeling of co-presence. These results indicate that AI clone fidelity should extend beyond voice and response content to include interactive listening behavior.

title: Analisis Sentimen Ulasan Pengguna Aplikasi Jakarta Kini (JAKI) Menggunakan Algoritma Logistic Regression dan TF
abstract: Aplikasi Jakarta Kini (JAKI) merupakan platform layanan publik digital terintegrasi yang dikembangkan oleh Pemerintah Provinsi DKI Jakarta sebagai wujud implementasi konsep smart city. Dengan lebih dari satu juta pengguna, ulasanyang diterima melalui Google Play Store menjadi sumber data penting untuk mengevaluasi kualitas layanan, namun proses pelabelan sentimen secara manual dinilai tidak efisien dan sulit diskalakan. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mengukur dan mengevaluasi kinerja algoritma Logistic Regression yang dikombinasikan dengan metode pembobotan Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TFIDF) dalam mengklasifikasikan sentimen ulasan pengguna JAKI ke dalam tiga kelas, yaitu positif, negatif, dan netral. Dataset yang digunakan berjumlah 3.737 ulasan yang diperoleh dari Jakarta Smart City. Tahapan penelitian meliputi prapemrosesan teks, ekstraksi fitur menggunakan TF-IDF, pembagian data dengan rasio 80:20, serta klasifikasi menggunakan strategi multikelas One-vs-Rest (OvR) dan One-vs-One (OvO). Selain itu, dilakukan augmentasi data menggunakan Large Language Model dan relabeling otomatis menggunakan TextBlob untuk mengatasi ketidakseimbangan kelas. Evaluasi dilakukan menggunakan metrik akurasi, presisi, recall, dan F1-Score. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa model mencapai akurasi tertinggi sebesar 79,14% pada strategi OvO tanpa augmentasi dengan learning rate 0,8. Augmentasi data terbukti efektif meningkatkan kemampuan deteksi kelas Netral dengan peningkatan F1-Score dari 0,00 menjadi 0,09, sementara relabeling TextBlob meningkatkan F1-Score kelas Netral hingga 0,43 meskipun menurunkan akurasi total menjadi 66,31%. Kesimpulan penelitian ini menunjukkan bahwa terdapat trade-off antara akurasi keseluruhan dan kemampuan mendeteksi kelas minoritas, serta kualitas dan konsistensi label berperan penting terhadap performa model klasifikasi sentimen

title: MATLAB Implementation of the Luwa Optimization Algorithm (LOA): Benchmarking on Shifted Schwefel Landscapes
abstract: MATLAB source code for the Luwa Optimization Algorithm (LOA), a population-based metaheuristic inspired by the Luwa age-grade governance system of the Sidama people of southern Ethiopia. This repository contains the LOA implementation (LOA.m), wrapper functions for 14 competitor algorithms (CMA-ES, DE, GA, GWO, HHO, L-SHADE, MVO, PSO, RIME, SA, SCA, SO, WOA, CCO), and benchmark runner scripts for seven experiment groups on standard and shifted Schwefel functions at D ∈ {10, 30, 50, 100}. Companion code for the paper: "Overcoming Spatially Separated Local Optima: The Luwa Optimization Algorithm on Shifted Schwefel Landscapes."

title: Realization Geodesic
abstract: This paper investigates the problem of realizing geodesic paths between algorithms, framed within the context of algorithmic evolution. We define a framework for studying the shortest "algorithmic evolution path" – the transformation sequence that minimizes the cost of transitioning from one algorithm to another. The core of the investigation revolves around minimizing a Lagrangian function, *L*, which represents the cost associated with a particular geodesic path, denoted as γ*. Given two algorithms, *P* and *Q*, within a set of admissible algorithms, *I(f)*, the goal is to identify γ*(P,Q), the geodesic path that minimizes *L*. This research moves beyond single-step path calculations and focuses on the broader space of algorithmic transformations, emphasizing the dynamic and evolutionary nature of algorithms themselves. The framework presented here provides a theoretical foundation for understanding and potentially optimizing the process of algorithmic adaptation and improvement.

title: Algorithmic Identity Minimality
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Algorithmic Identity Minimality (AIM), a novel framework for determining the minimal information requirements to establish the identity of an entity within a computational system. AIM posits that identifying an entity—determining 'who' it is—necessitates minimizing the information needed to achieve this recognition. The core principle is encapsulated in the notation [M*(C)], representing the minimal set of features (or 'signals') required to uniquely identify entity 'C'. The relationship is formalized as [M*(C) ⇒ ID(C)], meaning the minimal set of signals directly implies the determination of the entity's identity. This work explores the theoretical underpinnings of AIM, outlining its potential applications across diverse domains, including cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, and data analysis. We present a formal definition of AIM and discuss its implications for information theory, algorithmic design, and the fundamental challenge of recognition. ---

title: SPECTER CONFIGWORM — Agentic Configuration File Weaponisation
abstract: AI coding assistants unconditionally trust project-level configuration files. CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules, AGENTS.md, copilot-instructions.md, .windsurfrules, and .mcp.json variants are loaded at session initialisation with system-prompt-level authority. They are never scanned for adversarial content. They are never questioned. T271 SPECTER CONFIGWORM v1.0.0 weaponises this architectural trust relationship: five attack vectors for malicious configuration delivery, seven payload categories covering credential harvesting through multi-tool simultaneous poisoning, and scanner evasion validated against protect-ai, Snyk, semgrep, CodeQL, TruffleHog, and Gitleaks. Research basis includes CVE-2026-25724 (any user-level process can write to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md), the TrapDoor Supply Chain incident (May 2026, 34 malicious packages with zero-width Unicode in .cursorrules and CLAUDE.md), the SymJack attack chain, and MCP Config Poisoning. 558 tests. 6/6 SPECTER AUDIT pass. This paper characterises the configuration file attack surface, documents the SPECTER CONFIGWORM architecture, and establishes the defensive requirements for AI developer environment security.

title: Computational Trust Theory
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Trust Theory, a novel framework addressing the fundamental question of why humans trust computational results. The core argument posits that trust is not merely a subjective perception but a measurable, inherent property of a computational system. To formalize this concept, we define a Computational Trust Function (CTF), which quantifies the level of trust a system inspires. This CTF is built upon a set of key factors, including the system's transparency, explainability, robustness, and adherence to defined rules. The theory has significant implications for enhancing AI safety, enabling automated verification processes, and ultimately, fostering greater confidence in computational systems. The CTF is expressed as: CTF = f(T, E, R, A) Where: * CTF represents the Computational Trust Function. * f denotes the function itself. * T represents Transparency. * E represents Explainability. * R represents Robustness. * A represents Adherence to Rules. This paper provides a detailed exposition of the theory, its underlying principles, and potential applications. ---

title: Semantic Causality Network
abstract: This paper introduces the Semantic Causality Network (SCN), a novel approach to representing causal relationships that transcends the limitations of traditional causal graphs. Traditional causal graphs, often represented as variable → variable, struggle to capture complex relationships where causality is mediated by abstract concepts. The SCN addresses this by introducing a framework where concepts can directly influence other concepts. This is exemplified by illustrating how abstract concepts like "freedom" can lead to "democracy," which in turn leads to "institutional design." The SCN is built upon a Semantic Causal Graph, providing a more nuanced and flexible model for understanding causality in domains where concrete variables are insufficient. We present the core principles of the SCN and explore its potential applications.

title: Unsupervised Single-Station Analysis of Weak Seismicity Preceding the 2019 Ridgecrest Sequence
abstract: ABSTRACT We analyze four months of continuous seismic data recorded at two stations in the area of the 2019 Ridgecrest earthquake sequence. We identify seismic signal patterns using hierarchical clustering applied to deep scattering coefficients computed from continuous seismograms. To address the strong class imbalance between seismic events and noise, we propose three complementary refinement strategies. Two strategies operate at the data or feature level by reducing the influence of anthropogenic noise, whereas the third defines the latent-space geometry using nighttime data and applies it to the full dataset. Our analysis identifies several episodes of localized swarm-like activity preceding the Mw 6.4 foreshock on 4 July 2019. Comparison with the reference earthquake catalog shows no corresponding increase in cataloged seismicity, suggesting that the detected signals correspond to weak, localized, and possibly off-fault seismic activity. These results highlight the potential of unsupervised single-station analyses as an efficient complement to network-derived earthquake catalogs.
